en: The Lalitavistara Sūtra (Buddhacarita), Scroll One; also known as the *Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha*.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Descendant of the Ikṣvāku lineage, Śākya, the Invincible King,
Possessing pure wealth and complete virtue, he was thus named Śuddhodana.
All living beings delighted in gazing upon him, Like the newly risen moon.
The King was like Śakra, Lord of Devas; the Queen was like Śacī.
Her resolve was as stable as the earth, and her mind as pure as a lotus flower.
Though she is metaphorically named Māyā, in reality she is beyond compare.
Into that Elephant Queen, he descended as a spirit and dwelt within her womb.
His mother was entirely free from sorrow and affliction;
she harbored no thoughts of illusion or falsehood, detested the clamor of the mundane world, and delighted in dwelling in secluded forests.
The sublime garden of Lumbinī, with its flowing springs and luxuriant flowers and fruits, is tranquil and conducive to meditative reflection; I entreat the King to visit it.
The King, understanding her aspiration, conceived a sense of wonder.
He commanded his inner and outer retinues to go together to that grove.
At that time, Queen Māyā, knowing that her time of delivery had arrived,
lay reclined upon a secure and excellent couch, attended by hundreds of thousands of court ladies.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, when the pure and harmonious air was perfectly balanced,
he observed the fasts and cultivated pure virtue; the Bodhisattva was born from her right side,
a Great Compassionate One who saves the world, causing his mother no distress.
King Uruvilvā was born from the thigh; King Bimbisāra was born from the hand;
King Mandhātṛ was born from the crown of the head; King Kakravartin was born from the armpit.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: he was born emerging from the right side.
Gradually emerging from the womb, his radiance shines everywhere;
as if falling from the void, he does not pass through the birth canal.
Having cultivated merit for immeasurable kalpas, he knows of himself that he is born without dying.
Tranquil and unwavering, it is brilliant, wondrous, and majestic.
Shining forth from the womb, it is like the sun first rising;
its observation is exceedingly luminous, yet it does not harm the faculty of sight.
Though gazed upon, it does not dazzle, like the moon viewed in the sky;
The radiance of one’s own body outshines [all else], just as the sun eclipses the light of a lamp.
The true golden body of the Bodhisattva illuminates everywhere in this same way.
With a true mind undisturbed, he walked seven paces with steady composure;
beneath his feet were level soles, radiant and clear like the seven stars.
With the gait of the lion, king of beasts, he surveyed the four quarters.
Having realized the true meaning, one is capable of speaking thus:
"This birth is the birth of a Buddha; it is my final birth.
In this single life alone, I shall deliver all beings."
At that moment, from the midst of the void, two streams of pure water flowed down—
one warm and one cool— drenching his head and bringing joy to his body.
He was seated within a precious palace and lay upon a bed of lapis lazuli.
The Heavenly King with golden-flower hands Holds up the four legs of the throne.
The various devas in the air Hold precious canopies in attendance;
Receiving his majestic spiritual power, they offer praise And exhort him to realize the Buddha-way.
The dragon kings were filled with joy, thirsting for the sublime Dharma;
having served the Buddhas of the past, they now encountered this Bodhisattva.
Scattering mandārava flowers, they devotedly delighted in making offerings.
When the Tathāgata appears in the world, the Śuddhāvāsa devas rejoice;
having already abandoned the joy of desire, they exult for the sake of the Dharma,
so that sentient beings submerged in the ocean of suffering may attain liberation.
The Sumeru King of Jewel Mountains firmly sustains this great earth;
yet when a Bodhisattva appears in the world,
it is stirred by the wind of his merit until it trembles everywhere, like a boat tossed by the wind upon the waves.
Fine powdered sandalwood incense and lotus treasuries of myriad jewels drift through the air,
blown by the wind, scattering and falling in profusion;
celestial garments descend from the sky, and their touch brings sublime bliss to the body.
The sun and moon moved according to their usual courses, yet their radiance was doubled in brilliance;
the fires throughout the world blazed up spontaneously without fuel,
and cool wells of pure water appeared naturally before and behind them.
The ladies of the inner palace were struck with wonder and marveled at this unprecedented event;
they vied with one another to come and drink from and bathe in it, all giving rise to thoughts of peace and bliss.
Countless devas of the various heavens, delighting in the Dharma, gathered there like clouds.
Throughout the Lumbinī grove, amidst the dense foliage of the trees,
extraordinary and wondrous flowers bloomed out of season;
and all violent beings simultaneously gave rise to hearts of loving-kindness.
All diseases in the world, without treatment, are naturally cured;
all birds and beasts that cry out in disorder become tranquil and silent;
the ten thousand rivers all cease their flow, and turbid waters are all rendered clear.
The sky was free from clouds and mists, and celestial drums resounded spontaneously.
All the worlds attained peace and happiness,
as if a land beset by calamity had suddenly obtained a wise and enlightened ruler.
The reason the Bodhisattva was born was to rescue the world from its manifold sufferings;
it was only that King of Māras who trembled with great anxiety and distress.
When the Father King saw his son born, he marveled at this extraordinary and unprecedented event.
Though his natural disposition was calm and grave, he was so startled that his usual countenance changed;
two breaths rose within his chest, one of joy and one of fear.
When the lady saw her son, she realized he had not been born by the ordinary way.
Women are by nature timid and weak; filled with trepidation, they harbor feelings as conflicting as ice and fire.
Unable to distinguish between the signs of good and ill fortune, they instead give rise to further anxiety and fear.
Elder women and mothers-in-law become mutually confused, each praying to the spirits and deities.
Each requested their own tutelary deity, "We pray that the Prince may be at peace.
At that time, there was in that forest a Brahmin who understood the marks [of a great man],
possessed of dignified deportment and vast learning, endowed with eloquence and a high reputation.
Seeing these signs, his heart was filled with joy, a rapture such as he had never known before.
Perceiving that the king’s mind was struck with alarm, he addressed the king with the truth:
"When a person is born into this world, they seek only a preeminent son."
The King is now like the full moon; you should give rise to great joy.
Having now fathered this extraordinary son, he will surely bring glory to his lineage.
Settle your mind and rejoice within yourself; do not harbor any further doubts.
Auspicious signs gather for the family and the state; from now on, prosperity shall increase.
The extraordinary and sublime son born [to you] will surely be a savior of the world;
this body of the supreme being possesses a wondrous golden radiance.
With such sublime marks as these, you will surely attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment;
yet if you should delight in worldly life, you will surely become a Wheel-Turning King,
a sovereign of the entire earth who governs with courageous and righteous Dharma.
The King rules over the four continents, commanding all other kings;
just as among the lights of the world, the sunlight is supreme,
so too when dwelling in the mountain forests, he focuses his mind on seeking liberation.
Having accomplished true wisdom, he shines universally upon the world;
like Mount Sumeru, he is the sovereign king among all mountains.
Among all jewels, gold is supreme; among all streams, the ocean is supreme.
Among all constellations, the moon is supreme; among all luminaries, the sun is supreme.
So too, when the Tathāgata dwells in the world, he is supreme among those with two feet.
His pure eyes are long and wide; his upper and lower lashes blink like those of a majestic bull.
Gazing fixedly at the deep azure blue, brilliant and radiant like the shape of a half-moon—
how could this sign not be the eyes of one who is equal and supreme?
At that time, the King addressed the twice-born:
"By what causes and conditions do such extraordinary signs appear?
They ought not to manifest for a former king, yet they have appeared in my world.
The Brahmin addressed the King:
"One should not speak thus:
'Extensive learning and wisdom, reputation and one's undertakings—
regarding these four matters, one should not concern oneself with their sequence.'"
The nature of things arises, each originating from causes and conditions;
I shall now speak of various analogies, so listen attentively, O King.
Viśvāmitra and Aṅgiras—these two belong to the lineages of ṛṣis.
Having passed through many long ages, they each gave birth to sons of diverse natures.
Vṛhaspati and Śukra were able to compose treatises on kingship;
they did not descend from the lineage of former clans.
The sage Sārasa, though the scriptures and treatises had long been severed,
gave birth to Bāvarī, who continued to illuminate those scriptures and treatises.
The arising of present knowledge and vision does not necessarily depend upon one's ancestral lineage.
The Ṛṣi Vyāsa composed many sūtras and śāstras;
finally, his descendant Vaibhīṣika extensively collected verses and prose passages.
The Ṛṣi Ātreya did not understand the treatises on medical formulas.
In his next birth he was Adīla, who was well able to cure a hundred ailments;
in his second birth he was the seer Kuśika, who was not conversant with the treatises of the non-Buddhists;
later he was King Gātinna, who fully understood the doctrines of the non-Buddhists.
The Ikṣvāku dynasty, beginning with King Ikṣvāku, could not restrain the tides of the ocean;
but when it reached King Sagara, who fathered a thousand princes,
they were able to restrain the great ocean’s tides so that they did not exceed their usual limits.
The seer Jaṇṇaku attained the path of meditation without a teacher.
All who acquire renown do so through their own power;
some were superior at first and later inferior, while others were inferior at first and later superior.
Emperors and various deities do not necessarily inherit their lineage;
therefore, throughout all worlds, one should not regard priority or sequence.
Great King, now being thus, you should give rise to a heart of joy.
"Because my heart is filled with joy, I am forever free from doubt.
Having heard the seer’s words, the king rejoiced and increased his offerings, saying,
"I have now given birth to an excellent son who shall succeed me to the rank of a Wheel-Turning King."
My years are already advanced; having left the household life to cultivate the holy life, do not let the Prince of Sages abandon the world to wander in the mountain forests.
At that time, in a nearby grove, there was an ascetic seer.
Named Asita, he was skilled in the science of marks;
he came to the gate of the royal palace, where the king thought him to be Brahmā in person.
He delighted in asceticism and the True Dharma; these two characteristics were both manifest in him.
The King was greatly delighted by the prince’s perfect endowment of the marks of brahmacarya;
he immediately invited him into the palace and respectfully prepared offerings.
Leading him into the inner apartments, the King desired nothing more than to behold the prince.
Though surrounded by a multitude of court ladies, he dwells as if in a secluded forest;
seated upon the throne of the True Dharma, he is honored and served with reverence,
just as King Anādṛṣṭi was served by Vāsiṣṭha.
Then the king said to the seer:
"I have now attained great benefit.
I have troubled the Great Seer by humbling yourself to come and accept me."
"Whatever needs to be done, I pray that you will instruct me at the proper time.
Having thus made this request, the Great Sage was greatly delighted and said:
"Excellent, King Constantly Victorious! You are fully endowed with all virtues."
Delighting in those who come to seek aid, he bestows gifts and honors the True Dharma;
born of a noble clan distinguished by benevolence and wisdom, he is humble, respectful, and skillfully compliant.
Having cultivated many wondrous causes in past lives, these supreme fruits now manifest in the present.
You should listen as I explain the causes and conditions for my coming here today.
I have come by way of the sun’s path and heard the devas in the sky declare that the King has fathered a crown prince who shall attain the path of perfect enlightenment.
Having also seen these prior auspicious signs, I have now come here for this purpose:
to behold the King of the Śākyas as he raises the banner of the True Dharma.
Upon hearing the seer’s words, the king became certain and was freed from the net of doubt.
He ordered the Crown Prince to be brought out to be shown to the seer.
The seer observed the Prince: beneath his feet were wheels with a thousand spokes;
his fingers and toes were joined by webs; and between his eyebrows stood a white tuft of hair.
The horse’s private parts were well-concealed, its complexion radiant with brilliant light;
seeing this, he was struck by an unprecedented thought and shed tears with long sighs.
When the King saw the seer weeping, his heart trembled as he thought of his son.
Qi coagulated and filled his chest; with palpitations, he could not find peace.
Unconsciously rising from his seat, he prostrated at the feet of the Immortal and addressed him, saying:
Your countenance is exceedingly majestic; you are hardly different from a celestial being.
You say you are the foremost among men; why then do you give rise to sorrow and grief?
Is it not because of a short-lived son that you have produced this sorrow and grief in me?
Having long thirsted for the nectar of immortality, have you now lost it once again?
Is this not like losing one’s wealth and treasures, or the ruin of one’s family and the extinction of one’s state?
If there remains a superior son, the lineage of the nation has a place to which it may be entrusted.
At the time of my death, my mind shall be joyful, and I shall be born in peace and happiness in the next world;
just as a person with two eyes, one sleeps while the other remains awake.
Do not be like the flowers of autumn frost, which, though they bloom, bear no fruit.
Among one's kinsmen, none loves more deeply than a son.
You should grant me a timely prediction, so that I may find relief.
The Rishi, knowing that the father-king’s heart was filled with great anxiety and fear, [spoke].
He then addressed the Great King:
"I have already spoken to you previously, O Great King; be careful not to give rise to doubt yourself.
Now my appearance is just as it was before; you should not harbor any other thoughts."
Reflecting that my years have reached their end, I weep and sigh with deep sorrow.
Now, at this time of my passing, this son has appeared in the world;
he is born for the sake of ending all birth—such a person is difficult to encounter.
He renounced the rank of a noble wheel-turning monarch and, unattached to the realms of the five desires,
diligently practiced asceticism until he attained awakening and realized the truth.
For the sake of all living beings, he constantly extinguished the obstacles of delusion and darkness.
Forever blazing throughout the world, the sun of wisdom radiates its light.
Sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of suffering:
various ailments are the gathered foam, old age is the massive waves, and death is the great tidal surge.
Boarding the light boat of wisdom, one crosses the perils of these many currents;
with wisdom as the current flowing upstream, pure precepts serve as the banks.
Samādhi is the cool pond, and right concentration is the flock of wondrous birds.
Thus profound and vast is this great river of the True Dharma.
All sentient beings, parched by craving, drink from it and find relief;
yet they remain stained by attachment to the objects of the five desires, driven and oppressed by manifold sufferings.
Lost in the vast wilderness of birth and death, they know not where to turn;
the Bodhisattva appears in the world to open the path to liberation.
The fire of worldly desire blazes fiercely, with the objects of the senses as its fuel.
He raises the great cloud of compassion, raining down the Dharma rain to extinguish [suffering].
The door of delusion’s darkness has its heavy panels wide open, with greed and desire as its bolt;
it blocks all sentient beings from the gateway of liberation that leads to the essential way out.
With the tweezers of adamantine wisdom, he plucks out the thorns of craving and attachment.
Bound by the net of ignorance, beings suffer in poverty and misery with no refuge;
when the Dharma King appears in the world, he is able to untie the fetters of sentient beings.
"O King, do not give rise to grief or affliction on account of this son;
you should rather concern yourself with those sentient beings who are attached to desire and violate the True Dharma.
I am now ruined by old age and death, having become far removed from noble merit."
Though they may attain various meditative concentrations, they do not reap their benefits.
Having failed to hear the True Dharma from this Bodhisattva,
after the body perishes and life ends, they will surely be reborn in the Heaven of the Three Difficulties.
The king and his retinue, having heard what that seer said, understood that he was lamenting for himself; their terror was entirely dispelled.
"Having given birth to this extraordinary son, my heart has attained great peace."
"Having left the household life and renounced worldly glory, you have practiced the path of the seers;
thus you did not succeed to the royal throne, which has caused me displeasure.
At that time, the seer spoke these truthful words to the king:
"If it must be as Your Majesty fears, he shall surely attain the Way of Perfect Enlightenment.
Having comforted the hearts of those within Your Majesty’s retinue, he will,
by his own supernatural power, soar into the void and depart far away."
At that time, King Śuddhodana, seeing his son’s extraordinary marks and hearing the decisive and truthful words of Asita,
felt deep reverence for his son; he cherished and protected him while constantly keeping him in his thoughts.
A great amnesty is proclaimed throughout the world, and all those in prison are set free.
Regarding the worldly custom of giving birth to children, one may choose and adopt matters as appropriate,
following the various medical scriptures and treatises, performing every rite accordingly.
When ten days had passed since the birth of the son, his mind was at peace and settled;
he made offerings universally to all the heavenly deities and bestowed extensive alms upon those who possess the Way—
the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas— who offered prayers for his auspicious blessings.
He bestowed alms upon all his ministers, as well as the poor and destitute within the kingdom;
to the multitudes of village and city women, and to cattle, horses, elephants,
wealth, and coin— each according to their needs— he gave it all.
Having divined and chosen an auspicious time, the son was moved back to his original palace;
he partook of two meals and cleansed his teeth with white substances.
A palanquin adorned with the seven treasures was prepared, its various colored pearls interwoven, its brilliant flames of light exceedingly lustrous.
The Queen cradled the Prince and circumambulated the celestial deities.
Thereafter, they ascended the precious carriage, followed by a multitude of court ladies;
the King, along with his ministers and subjects, all escorted them in procession.
Just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, is surrounded by the hosts of gods,
or like Maheśvara, from whom the six-faced son suddenly appeared;
having prepared various kinds of requisites, they provided offerings and invited him to receive merit.
Now that Your Majesty has given birth to a crown prince, all preparations are likewise made.
When the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa begot Nalakuvara,
all the hosts of devas were filled with great joy.
Now that the King has fathered a crown prince in the kingdom of Kapilavastu,
all the people likewise rejoice. At that time,
within the house of King Śuddhodana, because a holy son had been born, [all were filled with joy].
His kinsmen were renowned as noble youths, and all his ministers were loyal and virtuous.
Elephants, horses, precious chariots, and the seven kinds of precious vessels of the state’s wealth increased daily in excellence, arising and gathering according to need.
Innumerable hidden treasures spontaneously emerge from the earth;
within the pure Snow Mountains, a wild herd of white elephants arrives of its own accord without being summoned,
and without a driver, they are naturally tamed.
Horses of various mixed colors, their forms exceedingly majestic;
with crimson manes and slender, long tails, they leap and gallop as swift as birds in flight.
Born of the wild, they arrive spontaneously in accordance with the season.
Pure-colored, well-trained oxen, Fat, strong, and of upright form, Walking with steady steps and yielding pure, fragrant milk, Have all assembled like clouds at the proper time.
Those who harbor enmity become even-minded; The indifferent grow more refined and sincere.
Natural bonds of kinship and intimacy grow ever more profound, and all disorder and rebellion are entirely eliminated.
Gentle breezes blow in harmony with the seasons, and rain falls at the proper time; thunder and lightning do not strike with violent force.
Planting no longer requires waiting for the right season, and the harvests gathered are doubly abundant.
The five grains are fresh, fragrant, and delicious; light, soft, and easy to digest.
For all those who are pregnant, their bodies are at ease and their physical condition harmonious and comfortable.
With the exception of those who have received the four noble lineages, all other people in the world [rely upon these].
Each person’s livelihood is as it should be, with no thought of seeking anything else.
Free from pride, stinginess, and envy, and likewise devoid of anger or malice,
all the men and women are profoundly identical to the people of the primordial kalpa.
Celestial temples and various monasteries, gardens, groves, wells, springs, and ponds—all will become like celestial objects, arising spontaneously according to the seasons.
Throughout the entire realm there shall be no hunger; the calamities of war and pestilence shall cease.
The people within the kingdom, relatives and kin, love and respect one another.
They delight in the joy of the Dharma and do not give rise to defiled desires;
they seek wealth through righteous means, without any heart for greedy profit.
Practicing giving for the sake of the Dharma, without seeking any thought of recompense;
cultivating the four Brahma-vihāras, he extinguished all thoughts of malice and harm.
In the past, King Maṇu gave birth to Prince Sūryaprabha.
The entire nation was blessed with auspiciousness, and all evils were stilled at once.
Now that the King has fathered a prince, his virtue is likewise so;
because he is endowed with the meaning of all virtues, he is named Siddhārtha.
At that time, Lady Māyā beheld the son she had borne,
as upright and handsome as a celestial youth, endowed with every excellence;
overcome by joy beyond measure, her life ended and she was reborn in the heavens.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, beholding the Prince— a celestial youth whose virtue and appearance were uniquely eminent in the world—
raised him with love after his biological mother had passed away,
as if he were her own son; the son likewise revered her as a mother.
Like the sun, moon, and the light of a fire, which shine from a faint glow to ever-widening radiance, so too does the Prince grow day by day; his virtue and appearance are likewise thus.
He is like priceless sandalwood incense and the renowned jewel of Jambūnada gold.
Divine elixirs for protecting the body adorn his person with necklaces;
the vassal states and neighboring kingdoms, hearing that the King has fathered a prince,
present him with various rare treasures, cattle, sheep, deer, horses, and chariots.
Jeweled vessels and ornaments served to delight the Prince's heart;
yet despite these various decorations and toys for infants,
the Prince was by nature calm and grave— his form young, but his mind mature.
His mind dwells in lofty and sublime realms, unstained by worldly glory;
he cultivates all arts and skills, surpassing his teachers upon hearing them but once.
When the King, his father, saw his profound intelligence, he deeply feared that he would transcend the mundane world.
He traveled extensively to seek among renowned noble clans those families distinguished by their moral character and propriety.
There was a maiden of upright and beautiful appearance named Yaśodharā;
she was to be betrothed as the Crown Prince’s consort, and he sought to win her heart through persuasion.
The Crown Prince’s aspirations are lofty and far-reaching; his virtue is abundant and his countenance clear and bright.
He is like the eldest son of Brahmā, Śanatkumāra.
The noble consort possesses a beautiful appearance, with a graceful, elegant, and refined bearing.
Resplendent and magnificent as a celestial queen, they dwell together in joy day and night.
For them, a pure palace was established, vast, beautiful, and most solemn;
it stands loftily in the void, stretching afar like autumn clouds.
Temperate and cool, the four seasons are harmonious; choose a fine dwelling according to the time.
Surrounded by a multitude of maidens who perform music in harmony with celestial melodies, do not dwell near impure sounds or sights, lest they give rise to thoughts of world-weariness.
In natural jewel palaces, celestial maidens play heavenly music;
its sounds and sights dazzle the eyes and mind.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in lofty palaces, their music is likewise so.
Dwelling in tranquility, cultivate pure virtue; transform others through benevolence and the True Dharma.
Associate with the worthy and distance yourself from evil friends; let the mind be unstained by affection and love.
Regard sensual desires as poisonous thoughts; restrain the emotions and guard the sense faculties.
He eliminates frivolity of mind, listens to litigations with a serene countenance,
and through compassionate instruction, satisfies the hearts of the multitude.
He cuts off all arts of conspiracy and rebellion, and teaches the methods for saving the world.
The myriad people attained peace and happiness.
The myriad people were likewise thus: they served fire and venerated various deities, joining their palms and drinking the moonlight.
Bathing his mind in the water of the Dharma, he prays for blessings not for himself alone, but solely for you and the myriad people.
His righteous words are not without love; his loving words are not without truth.
Truthful speech is not unloving;
one cannot speak according to reality regarding objects of love or non-love without relying on the perceptions of greed and hatred.
To settle disputes with impartiality and not to hold assemblies for sacrifices to heaven brings greater merit than adjudicating legal cases.
To bestow abundant gifts beyond one's expectations and to have no thoughts of conflict in the mind—
Subdue enemies through virtue;
abandon the seven and restrain the five. Attain the three awakenings and realize the three;
know the two and relinquish the two.
One should show compassion and forbearance toward those facing death, refrain from using harsh or evil words,
and instruct them with gentle speech; one should strive to bestow material goods and point out the path for sustaining life,
while they receive instruction in the way of the immortals.
Having extinguished the mind of enmity and resentment, his fame and virtue spread far and wide;
worldly afflictions were forever eliminated.
Throughout the land, all followed and practiced his example, until the hearts of people became as tranquil as still waters.
The four limbs and all the sense organs followed their course.
At that time, Prince Śuddhodana and the noble consort Yaśodharā both grew gradually older; she conceived and gave birth to Rāhula.
King Śuddhodana thought to himself: "The Prince has now fathered a son;
as generations succeed one another, the True Teaching shall have no end.
Since the Prince has fathered a son, his love for this child is equal to my own."
I no longer worry about leaving the household life; I shall simply cultivate goodness with all my might.
Now my mind is profoundly at peace, no different from the bliss of being born in heaven, like that of the royal sages dwelling on the Path at the beginning of the eon.
One who practices pure deeds with love, performs sacrifices without harming living beings,
and zealously cultivates sublime actions— such a king excels, such a one excels in the holy life (brahmacarya).
He excels among his kinsmen, excels in wealth and treasures, and excels in valor and skillful arts.
Clearly illuminating the world, like the thousand rays of the sun;
for this reason he is a king, so as to manifest his son;
manifesting the son is for the sake of the clan, and bringing glory to the clan through renown.
Through high renown one attains birth in heaven; having attained birth in heaven, one experiences joy;
with that joy, wisdom increases; awakening to the Way, one propagates the True Dharma.
Having first gained superior fame, one receives and practices the manifold wondrous paths.
I only pray that the Crown Prince, this beloved son, will not abandon his home;
for all kings whose sons are still young do not allow their kingdoms to worry about their hearts becoming dissolute.
Indulging his passions and attached to worldly pleasures, he was unable to continue the royal lineage.
Now that the King has fathered a crown prince, the prince indulges in the five desires according to his heart's wish;
he desires only the glory of the world and does not wish to study the Path.
The Bodhisattva-kings of the past, though their Way was profound and firm,
yet first cultivated worldly glory and pleasure, begetting sons to succeed to the lineage,
and only thereafter entered the mountain forests to practice the path of silent stillness.
Outside are various gardens and groves, with flowing springs and cool ponds;
Diverse trees of flowers and fruits stand in rows, casting deep shadows below.
Birds of many different species soar and sport within them.
The four kinds of flowers, both aquatic and terrestrial, blaze with color and waft exquisite fragrances.
As the maidens perform music, their lutes and songs inform the Prince.
Hearing this music, the Prince marvels at the beauty of that grove.
Internally harboring great joy and delight, he longed for an excursion to view the world;
like a tethered mad elephant, he always yearned for the vast wilderness.
When the royal father heard that the Crown Prince wished to go out to that garden for a stroll, he [permitted it].
He immediately commanded his ministers to prepare the ceremonial regalia with full splendor;
they leveled and purified the royal road, removing all that was unsightly and foul,
as well as those who were aged, diseased, deformed, infirm, or suffering from poverty.
Lest my young son, who brings me little joy, should see this and give rise to a heart of revulsion.
Having completed all the preparations for his adornment, he rose to request leave and bid farewell.
When the King saw the Prince arrive, he stroked his head and gazed upon his countenance.
Sorrow and joy entwine within their hearts; they grant their word with their mouths, yet their minds remain behind.
Their carriage is adorned with various precious ornaments, drawn by four horses galloping smoothly over level ground.
They are virtuous and skilled in the arts, young and of beautiful countenance.
With exquisite, pure, and fresh flowers for garments, they drive together in a single carriage.
Flowers are scattered throughout the streets and alleys; jeweled canopies cover the roadside.
Trees line the sides of the path, and precious vessels serve as adornments.

Having planted the roots of virtue in past lives, you have obtained these exquisite provisions.

At that time, the Prince heard the friend Udāyin’s sweet words and clever eloquence,

Sleepless and unattached to desires, Unbroken and not disparaging others,
