saw those men and women whose agitation was unlike their usual demeanor;
he commanded a foreigner to be summoned and questioned him thoroughly regarding the cause and conditions.
Prostrating respectfully beneath the king’s tower, he fully reported what he had seen and heard:
"I have heard that among the Śākya clan there was an extraordinary and most excellent son, whose divine wisdom transcended the world;
he ought to lead the king over the eight directions."
Now that he has gone forth and dwells here, all the people welcome him with reverence.
When the King heard this, his heart was filled with wonder and joy; though his body remained, his spirit had already sped forth.
He commanded his messengers to return quickly to observe the prince’s movements and conduct.
Following him closely in accordance with his instructions, I observed his every action.
With a mind serene and eyes steady, he moved with measured steps, manifesting the true deportment of a sage.
Entering the village to beg for food, he became the light for all mendicants.
Restraining his form, his mind was undisturbed; in both good and evil, he found no unease.
Whether the food was fine or coarse, he accepted whatever he received; holding his bowl, he returned to the secluded forest.
Having finished eating, he rinsed his mouth in the clear stream, delighting in stillness upon the White Mountain.
The green forest stands apart from the high cliffs, with crimson flowers blooming amidst them;
peacocks and various other birds wheel through the air, crying out in discordant harmony.
The dharma robes enhance the brilliance, like the sun shining upon Mount Fusang.
He sent someone to see him dwelling there, who returned with a full account of what had been heard in succession.

Upon hearing this, the king’s heart was filled with reverence; he immediately ordered his carriage to be prepared and set out, wearing his celestial crown and flowered robes, walking with the gait of a lion king.
Discerning all that is ancient and weighty, a man of tranquil composure and profound discernment,
leading a retinue of hundreds of thousands, ascended the White Mountain like a rising cloud.
Beholding the Bodhisattva’s majestic deportment, his sensory faculties were utterly serene.
Sitting upright in a mountain cave, like the moon adorning the clear blue sky;
with a wondrous form pure and dignified, as if the Dharma-body or Nirmanakaya,
a reverent heart arose solemnly, and he approached with respectful steps.
Just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, approached Maheśvara,
composed his countenance and observed the proper etiquette, respectfully inquiring after his well-being;
so too did the Bodhisattva move with deliberate grace, responding in accordance with the other’s conduct.
When the King had finished his greetings of courtesy, he sat upright upon a pure stone;
gazing intently at the divine countenance, his features softened and his heart filled with joy.
"I have humbly heard that your name is exalted within a noble clan, and that your magnificent virtue has been passed down through generations."
My feelings of admiration have long been accumulated; now I wish to resolve my doubts.
The primal source of the Sun-like dynasty has enjoyed its mandate for ten thousand generations;
that its virtuous legacy continues through the successor, and its vast influence gathers anew in this present age.
Wise and bright, yet so young in years—why have you left the household life?
A noble prince who transcends the world, why do you beg for food instead of seeking glory?
Your exquisite body deserves to be anointed with fragrant unguents; why do you wear the saffron robe?
Your hands ought to grasp the whole world, yet instead you receive but a meager meal;
if you do not succeed your father-king by receiving the abdication and enjoying his lands,
I shall now divide my own kingdom with you, hoping thus that you will show some regard for it.
Having already avoided the suspicion of pressuring one's kin, when the time passes, follow wherever you may go;
you should take to heart my sincere words and cherish virtue as a good neighbor.
Or perhaps you rely on a prestigious lineage, possessing both talent and virtue as well as a handsome appearance.
I do not wish to lower my lofty principles Or bend down to receive the kindness of others.
One should provide brave and capable men, With weapons and military provisions to follow;
If one gathers them in through one's own strength, Who in all under heaven would not offer their support?
The wise know the time to take; thus the wealth of Dharma and the five desires increase.
If one does not obtain these three benefits, one’s diligent efforts from beginning to end will be in vain.
Honor the Dharma and renounce wealth and beauty; for wealth belongs only to those who possess it.
Wealth, resources, renunciation, and the desire for the Dharma—these are what preserve one’s material sustenance.
If one is impoverished and forgets the Dharma, who could find joy in the five desires?
Therefore, when these three matters are present together, virtue flows and the Way is proclaimed.
Endowed with the wealth of Dharma and the five desires, he is called a great man in the world;
let not this body of perfect marks labor in vain without merit.
As the Mandhātrī Cakravartin King, he ruled over the four continents under heaven.
Śakra shared half his seat with you, yet in power you could not rule the heavens.
Now that your long, muscular arms are sufficient to grasp the realms of both men and gods,
I do not rely on royal force to compel you to stay by force.
Seeing your transformed appearance and how you cherish the robes of renunciation,
I already revere your virtue; moved by compassion for your hardships and pity for your person,
now that I see you going about begging, I wish to offer you this land.
In youth one experiences the five desires; in middle age one practices the use of wealth.
When old and the faculties have matured—this is the time for conforming to the Dharma.
If one guards wealth through the vigor of youth, one will surely be ruined by desire.
In old age, the vital energy becomes weak and subtle; one should follow this state to seek tranquility and silence.
An elder feels shame regarding wealth and desire; practicing the Dharma, he is honored by the whole world.
In youth, the mind is light and fickle, racing through the realms of the five desires.
Companionship with fellow practitioners is bound by deep bonds; their mutual affection is profound.
As years pass, those who lack such ties find little comfort; thus, those who follow the Dharma take this as their primary principle.
They entirely renounce the five desires, increasing instead their resolve for the Dharma.
Possessing the kingly dharma, he shall hold a great assembly to honor the celestial deities;
riding upon the back of a divine dragon, he will enjoy bliss as he ascends to heaven.
Like the victorious sage-kings of old, his body is adorned with precious necklaces and ornaments.
He established great assemblies for sacrificial offerings, believing they would ultimately lead to the reception of heavenly blessings.
Thus King Bimbisāra spoke through various skillful means,
yet the Prince’s resolve remained firm and unshakable, like Mount Sumeru.
King Bimbisāra followed along, having offered consolation and exhortation;
the Prince respectfully replied in thanks:
"You have well attained what is appropriate for the world; what you have said does not deviate from reason."
Hārita was of noble lineage and served as a virtuous friend to others;
with a mind of profound sincerity and humility, he spoke the Dharma in this manner.
The world speaks of the common masses who are unable to abide in benevolence and righteousness.
Those of meager virtue encounter only worldly passions; how could they comprehend such renowned and sublime matters?
Having inherited the excellent tradition of our ancestors, we honor propriety and cultivate respect and deference;
thus, amidst suffering and hardship, we provide for one another and do not abandon each other.
This is the mark of a true spiritual friend in the world:
one who generously distributes the wealth of a good companion. This is called a secure treasury;
whereas hoarding and guarding for one's own private profit will surely lead to swift ruin.
National wealth is not a constant treasure; giving it away is a meritorious deed.
When one gives both to others and to virtuous friends, there is no regret even after the wealth has been dispersed.
Knowing your profound sincerity, I shall not engage in contrary arguments.
Moreover, based on what I have seen, I shall speak to you with all my heart:
fearing birth, old age, sickness, and death, and desiring true liberation,
how could one who has abandoned kin and severed affection return to indulge in the five desires?
I do not fear fierce venomous snakes, nor freezing lightning or raging fires;
I only fear the objects of the five desires, which cause my mind to wander in toil.
The five desires are impermanent thieves that plunder the precious jewels of human goodness.
Deceitful and false, unreal and insubstantial, they are like conjured illusions.
To contemplate them for even a moment causes confusion; how much more so to dwell within them constantly?
The five desires are a great hindrance, forever obstructing the dharma of quiescent extinction.
Even celestial pleasures are not to be desired, let alone the desires of the human realm.
The five sensual desires give rise to craving; there is never a time when they are satisfied.
They are like a fierce fire fanned by a gale; even with the addition of fuel, it is never quenched.
Among all things in the world that are not beneficial, none surpasses the realm of the five desires.
Because sentient beings are deluded and greedy, they delight in attachment and remain unaware;
the wise fear the five desires and do not fall into what is not beneficial.
Though the king ruled over the four seas within, he still sought further beyond;
like the great ocean of craving and desire, it never knows the time of satiety.
When King Māndhātṛ, the Wheel-Turning Monarch, rained down gold upon the whole world,
The King ruled over the four continents, yet still aspired to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
when Śakra offered him half his seat, he sought to usurp it and met his end.
Aṅga practiced austerities and became king of the thirty-three heavens.
Though his mind was haughty with desire, the seer pulled the chariot by its steps;
because of such heedless conduct, he immediately fell among the pythons and snakes.
King Kṛkarāṭa, while wandering in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, [fell likewise].
He took a celestial maiden as his queen and levied taxes upon the sages' gold;
the sages, filled with resentment, cast a curse, whereby the kingdom was destroyed and he met his end.
The Great King Brahmā, the Great King Indra, and the Great King Agniṣvātta.
Nongsha returned to Śakra; how could the Lord of Devas possess permanence?
The realm is not solid; it is inhabited only by those of great power.
Clad in garments of grass, they eat fruit and drink from flowing springs.
With long hair hanging to the ground, silent and seeking nothing,
though he practiced such asceticism, he was ultimately ruined by desire.
One should know that the objects of the five desires are the enemies of those who practice the Path.
The mighty King Sahastrabhuja, valiant and difficult to oppose,
was slain by the seer Rāma precisely because of his craving for desire.
How much more so for me, of the Kṣatriya caste, who am not led astray by desire?
The desire for objects of scant flavor increases as one’s offspring grow;
this is what the wise loathe—who would consume the poison of desire?
Seeking various gains through manifold sufferings, all are driven by greed.
If one is free from desire, suffering does not arise.
The wise see the fault in suffering and eliminate desire;
what the world calls good is, in truth, entirely unwholesome.
Because sentient beings crave and delight in [sensual pleasures], they give rise to various forms of heedlessness;
through this heedlessness, they instead injure themselves, and at death, they shall fall into the evil realms.
That which is obtained through diligent application and protected by skillful means—
Through lack of diligence, one loses them of one's own accord; they cannot be retained by mere expedients.
Just like borrowed goods, the wise do not crave or cling to them;
yet through craving, one seeks with arduous toil, and upon obtaining them, increases one's attachment.
When there is extreme separation, suffering and affliction increase all the more;
like one who holds a torch and burns himself, the wise do not cling to such things.
Foolish and base people, their hearts burned by the poison of stinginess and greed, [suffer thus].
One undergoes suffering for a lifetime, never attaining peace or joy.
Greed and anger are like the venom of a snake; how could a wise person draw near to them?
They are like laboriously gnawing on a dry bone—lacking flavor and failing to satisfy.
One merely exhausts one's own teeth; this is what the wise do not taste.
Divided by kings, thieves, water, and fire, or shared with wicked sons as common property, it is like a piece of stinking meat, over which a flock of birds contends.
Craving for wealth is likewise so; it is not what the wise delight in.
Where wealth is accumulated, much enmity and hatred arise;
one must guard it day and night, like a person fearing a formidable enemy.
To be executed beneath the execution post in the eastern market is what human sentiment abhors;
yet the long posts of greed, anger, and delusion are what the wise always distance themselves from.
To enter into mountains, forests, rivers, and seas leads mostly to ruin and little peace.
Like fruit on the high branches of a tree, one who greedily seeks to grasp it often falls to their death;
the realm of sensual desire is just like this— though seen, it is difficult to seize.
Seeking wealth through painful means, it is hard to accumulate and easy to lose.
Just as that which is obtained in a dream, how could a wise person maintain it?
Like a false pit of fire covered over, the one who treads upon it will surely be burned to death;
the fire of craving is just like this, a place where the wise do not travel.
Just as Kūlavālaka, Piṅgiya, Nanda, Māṭhara,
and Caṇḍa were like the butcher’s knife and block,
so too is the form of sensual desire; it is not practiced by the wise.
Binding one's body to throw oneself into water or fire,
or casting oneself from high cliffs in pursuit of celestial bliss— these bring only suffering and yield no benefit.
Sūṇatapa and Sūṇāsa, the brothers Asurinda, [all perished thus].
Those born together love and cherish one another, yet they seek to slaughter one another;
when the body dies, the name perishes as well—all this is due to the cause of craving.
Greed and attachment make a person lowly, subjecting them to the suffering of being driven by whips and staves.
Craving and base hopes weary the body and spirit through the long night.
Deer die for their greed for sound; birds follow their greed for color;
fish in the deep waters crave the hook and bait—all are thus entangled by desire.
One observes that the requisites for life are not things of sovereign power:
food is taken to treat the affliction of hunger, and water is drunk to remove thirst;
clothing wards off wind and cold, and bedding serves to remedy sleepiness.
One seeks a vehicle because of the fatigue of travel; one seeks a bed and seat because of standing weariness.
One bathes to remove impurities; all these are for the sake of ceasing suffering.
Therefore, one should know that the five desires do not bring mastery.
Just as a person afflicted with a fever seeks cooling medicines to treat it,
the fool, greedily seeking to stop suffering, claims to have attained mastery.
Yet those very means of livelihood do not necessarily bring an end to suffering.
Furthermore, it causes the nature of suffering to increase; therefore, it is not a sovereign dharma.
Warm clothing is not constant bliss; when the time passes, it too gives rise to suffering.
Moonlight is cool in summer, yet in winter it increases the suffering of cold.
Even the eight worldly concerns are entirely devoid of fixed characteristics;
since the nature of suffering and pleasure is uncertain, how could there be any distinction between a slave and a king?
It is because he issues commands that the multitude obeys and employs them, and thus the king is regarded as superior.
Commands are themselves suffering, like bearing a heavy burden.
Weighing the light and heavy of the world, all manner of sufferings gather upon his person;
as a king, he has many enemies and hatreds, and even those close to him may become a source of affliction.
Having no kin and standing alone, what joy can there be in this?
Though one might rule over the four quarters of the world, its utility does not exceed that of a single person;
to strive for ten thousand affairs is but empty suffering—what benefit is it to the self?
It is better to cease greedy seeking and bring affairs to rest for the sake of great peace.
To dwell in the pleasures of a king’s five desires is not as joyful as the delight of sovereign tranquility.
Since joy is equal in both cases, what use is there for the position of a king?
Do not employ skillful means to lead me toward the five desires;
what my heart aspires to is the path of cool serenity and emptiness.
If you wish to benefit me, assist me in accomplishing that which I seek.
I do not fear my enemies, nor do I seek the pleasures of rebirth in heaven.
My mind harbors no attachment to worldly gain; thus, I have cast aside my celestial crown.
For this reason, I oppose your wishes and shall not follow your command.
Like one who has escaped the mouth of a venomous snake, how could they ever take hold of it again?
Holding a torch and burning oneself—how could one not quickly cast it aside?
Those with eyes envy the blind; having attained liberation, they seek bondage once more.
If the wealthy wished for poverty, and the wise practiced folly—
if such people existed in the world, then I would delight in that land.
Desiring to cross over birth, old age, and death, I restrain my body and practice begging for food.
With few desires and abiding in solitude, one avoids the evil realms in future lives;
thus there is peace in both worlds. You should not grieve for me now;
rather, you should pity those who rule as kings, whose hearts are ever empty and parched with craving.
Finding no peace in this life, you will suffer the retribution of pain in the next.
You, who belong to a renowned and noble lineage and possess the decorum of a great man,
have dwelt with me with deep affection, delighting in worldly pleasures as we shared them together.
I too should repay his kindness by exhorting you to share in my benefit;
if one practices the three kinds of pleasure, he is called a man of the world.
This, however, is not the true goal, for there is never satiety in constant seeking.
If one is free from birth, old age, and death, Only then is one called a Great Man.
You say that when young one is fickle and restless, And that one should leave the household life upon growing old;
But I see those who are advanced in years, Their strength diminished and unable to endure anything.
It is not as it was in the prime of youth, when one’s will was fierce and the mind resolute.
Now the Thief of Death follows with sword in hand, constantly watching for an opportunity;
how can you allow yourself to reach old age before finally fulfilling your resolve to leave the household life?
Impermanence is the hunter; old age is the bow and disease the sharp arrow.
In the wilderness of birth and death, it constantly lies in wait for the deer that are sentient beings;
seizing the opportunity, it cuts short their lives—who then can enjoy a full span of years?
Regarding the deeds of worldly people— whether matters of birth or death,
whether young, old, or middle-aged— all should diligently apply skillful means.
To perform sacrifices and cultivate great assemblies is entirely due to ignorance.
One should revere the True Dharma; yet instead, they kill to sacrifice to the heavens.
To seek blessings by harming living beings—such people lack compassion.
Even if the harm to living beings were to yield permanent results, one still ought not to kill.
How much more so when seeking impermanence, one harms living beings for the sake of sacrificial offerings?
If one lacks precepts, learning, and wisdom, yet practices meditative tranquility,
such a person should not follow worldly custom by performing sacrifices or establishing great assemblies.
Though killing may bring pleasure in this life, the wise should not kill;
how much less should one kill living beings in pursuit of merit in future lives?
The conditioned fruits of the three realms are none of them pleasing to me.
The phenomena of the various realms of existence flow and drift like grass swept away by wind and water;
therefore, I have come from afar to seek true liberation.
I have heard that there is an Arhat who skillfully explains the path to liberation.
Now I shall go to that place, where the Great Sage, the Muni, resides.
With sincere words, I suppress and sever my sorrow; I now offer my apologies to you.
May your kingdom be peaceful and secure, and may you protect it well as Śakra does.
His wisdom shines upon the world like the radiance of the blazing sun.
This preeminent lord of the earth maintains his life with an upright mind and protects his subjects through righteous transformation, ruling the world as a Dharma King.
Ice and snow have fire as their enemy; conditioned by fire, banners of smoke arise.
From these banners of smoke, floating clouds are formed; from the floating clouds, a great rain falls.
There is a bird in the midst of the sky that drinks the rain but does not let it fall upon its own body.
One who slays a grievous enemy makes that enemy his home; one who dwells in a home makes the home his grievous enemy.
You who would slay a grievous enemy, you should now subdue him so that he may attain liberation, just as one drinks rainless water to quench thirst.
Then the king joined his palms, and with a heart joyful in reverence for the Virtuous One, said:
"May that which you seek be swiftly fulfilled;
once you have quickly attained your goal, you shall surely return to take me under your care."
The Bodhisattva granted his consent within his heart, vowing to fulfill your wish;
having taken their leave, they followed the road together and proceeded toward Ārāḍa.
The King, along with his retinue, joined their palms and escorted him for some distance.
All conceived thoughts of wonder and returned to the city of Rājagṛha.
The descendant of the Ikṣvāku line, whose lineage was like moonlight,
arrived at that tranquil forest and respectfully approached the Muni, the great seer Ārāḍa.
The son of the noble Kālāma clan, seeing the Bodhisattva approaching from afar, raised his voice in praise from a distance and comforted him, saying, "Welcome.
With palms joined in reverent salutation, he inquired after his well-being: "Are you at peace?"
When their mutual inquiries were concluded, they sat down with composed decorum.
Upon seeing the Crown Prince’s dignified countenance and solemn bearing,
the brahmin was bathed by his virtue and bowed down, like one who drinks nectar when parched with thirst.
Raising his hand, he addressed the Prince:
"Sever the shackles of affectionate attachment, Just as an elephant sheds its tether;
With profound wisdom and the light of awakening, One can escape these poisonous fruits."
In ancient times, illustrious and victorious kings relinquished their thrones to their sons,
just as a person casts aside a withered flower garland once it has faded;
yet you, in the prime of your youth, have not accepted the position of a noble king.
Observing your profound and firm resolve, you are fit to be a vessel for the True Dharma;
you shall board the ship of wisdom and cross over the ocean of birth and death.
When ordinary people are enticed to come and study, I examine their talents before providing instruction.
"I now know that your resolve is firm and determined;
you may practice as you wish, for I shall never conceal anything from you.
Hearing these instructions, the Prince replied with joy:
"With an impartial mind, you have instructed me well without love or hatred;
simply receive this with an open heart, and your wish shall be fulfilled.
It is like one traveling at night who finds a torch, or a wanderer lost in direction who receives guidance."
Just as one who crosses the sea obtains a light boat, so am I now.
Having now received your compassionate permission, I venture to ask of what I doubt:
how may the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death be escaped?
At that time, Ārāḍa, having heard the questions posed by the Prince, explained them briefly for him based on his own various sūtras and śāstras:
"You are a man of keen insight, the foremost among the intelligent; [I shall explain it to you]."
Now listen as I explain the meaning of the arising and ceasing of birth and death.
Nature undergoes transformation into birth, old age, and death; these five constitute sentient beings.
"Nature" refers to pure essence, while "transformation" refers to the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*).
My awakening and my vision change according to the objects and the faculties;
form, sound, smell, taste, and touch—these are called the objects.
The hands, feet, speech, and the two [excretory] passages—these five are called the faculties of action.
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body—these are called the faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*).
The faculty of mind (*manendriya*) possesses two meanings: it is both karma and it is called sensation.
With the transformation of its nature as the cause, that which knows the cause is the self (*ātman*).
The seer Kapila, together with his disciples and retinue,
studied this essential meaning of mine and attained liberation.
That Kapila is now Prajāpati.
To be aware of birth, old age, and death—this is called "seeing.
That which is contrary to this is called "not seeing.
Ignorance, karma, and craving—these are said to be the turning of the wheel.
If one abides in these three types [of views], such sentient beings do not depart from them;
they lack faith, harbor doubts and confusion, fail to discern, and possess no skillful means.
They are deeply attached to their objective spheres and remain entangled in the notion of "mine."
Lacking faith, they revolve in perversion; their actions differ and their understandings differ.
When one says, "I speak," "I know," "I perceive," "I go," "I come," or "I abide"—such reckonings of a self are called the revolution of the "I-maker."
To waver regarding various natures, failing to ascertain whether they are so or not,
and thus remaining undecided— this is called doubt.
If it is said that "the self" is the dharma, then it is said that this is the mind.
It is also said that there is awakening and karma, and various enumerations further speak of a self.
Not making such distinctions is called "comprehensive inclusion" (*saṃgraha*);
not understanding [the distinctions between] the natures of the ignorant and the wise, or their transformations and so forth, is called "non-distinction" (*apṛthaktva*).
Worshiping and reciting various scriptures, sacrificing living beings at celestial shrines,
and regarding water, fire, and the like as means of purification— yet conceiving of these as liberation:
such various views as these are called "lack of skillful means."
That which is clung to by ignorance— the mental, verbal, and sensory activities,
as well as the clinging to sense objects— is called "attachment.
To regard all things as "mine" is called "appropriation."
These eight kinds of afflictions pervade the cycle of birth and death;
the foolish people of all worlds are gripped by the five fetters:
darkness and ignorance, as well as great delusion, anger, and fear.
Laziness is called darkness; birth and death are called delusion.
Craving and desire are called great delusion, for they cause great beings to give rise to confusion.
To harbor resentment is called hatred; to have fear in one's heart is called terror.
These ignorant worldlings are attached to the five desires, the root of the great suffering of birth and death, as they transmigrate through the five realms of existence.
Through successive births, they conceive the view of self, thinking: "I see," "I hear," "I know," and "I act."
Because of this reckoning of a self, one follows the stream of birth and death.
Since this cause lacks intrinsic nature, its fruit likewise lacks intrinsic nature;
this refers to right reflection, the four factors that lead toward liberation.
The wise and the ignorant, the manifest and the unmanifest—
if one understands these four dharmas, one can leave behind birth, old age, and death. When birth, old age,
and death are exhausted, one attains the state of the inexhaustible.
"The world's brahmins all rely upon this principle to practice the holy life (brahmacarya), and they also explain it extensively for others.
Upon hearing these words, the Prince again questioned Ārāḍa:
“What is the means?
To what ultimate point does it lead?
What kind of holy life (brahmacarya) is to be practiced?”
Furthermore, for how long should one continue?
For what purpose does one cultivate the holy life?
To what destination should the Dharma lead?
"Please explain these essential points to me in their entirety. Then,
Ārāḍa, according to the teachings of the sūtras and śāstras,
and by means of his own wisdom and skillful methods, further analyzed them in brief:
"First departing from the world to enter the homeless life, relying upon alms-gathering,
extensively gathering all dignified deportments, and upholding the true precepts.
With few desires and contentment, accepting whatever food is obtained, whether fine or coarse."
Delighting in solitude and practicing in seclusion, he diligently studies the various sūtras and śāstras.
Seeing the fearfulness of desire and the coolness of detachment from desire,
he restrains the village of the sense faculties and settles his mind in silent stillness.
Free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, And from the various afflictions of the desire realm,
One attains the joy and bliss born of seclusion, Obtaining the first dhyāna with vitarka and vicāra.
Having attained the bliss of the first dhyāna, As well as the mind of vitarka and vicāra,
Giving rise to thoughts of wonder, the foolish mind delights in attachment;
yet the mind that relies on the joy of seclusion, at the end of life, is reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
The wise are able to know this for themselves, employing skillful means to bring stillness to both vitarka and vicāra.
Diligently seeking higher progress, one attains the second dhyāna;
Relishing that joy and bliss, one is reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Through skillful means, one leaves behind joy and bliss, And further cultivates the third dhyāna.
Seeking no further excellence in bliss, one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven;
having relinquished even that mental delight, one attains the fourth dhyāna.
When both suffering and pleasure have ceased, one may conceive the notion of liberation.
Relying on the retribution of those four dhyānas, one is born in the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala);
because their lifespan is so long, it is called "Vast Results.
Upon arising from that meditative concentration, one perceives the body as a fault.
Advancing in the cultivation of wisdom, he felt weary of and detached from the fourth dhyāna.
Resolutely advancing in his quest, he employed skillful means to eliminate desire for form,
beginning with the various apertures of his own body, gradually cultivating the understanding of emptiness.
In the end, the stage of firmness is fully accomplished through the contemplation of emptiness;
having briefly observed the sphere of emptiness, one advances to contemplate immeasurable consciousness.
Being skillful in internal tranquility, one is free from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self."
Observing that nothing exists is the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
When flesh, skin, and bone have separated, like a wild bird released from its cage,
one who has distanced themselves from sense objects is liberated in just the same way.
This is the supreme brāhmaṇa, who has transcended form and is eternally inexhaustible;
the wise should know that this is true liberation.
As for the skillful means you asked about, as well as the seeker of liberation—
As I have explained above, those with deep faith should train accordingly.
The seer Kiṃśuka, as well as Janaka, Vidhūra, and other seekers of the Way—
"All have followed this path And attained true liberation.
Upon hearing their words, the Prince contemplated their meaning;
the karmic conditions of his past lives were awakened, and he questioned them once more:
"I have heard your superior wisdom concerning the subtle, profound, and minute meaning;
yet to know the cause and not abandon it is not the ultimate path.
To claim that liberation consists in the knowledge of the transformation of nature—this is your teaching."
I observe that this phenomenon of birth is also a phenomenon of seeds.
You claim that my purity constitutes true liberation;
yet if one encounters the convergence of causes and conditions, one should return once more to bondage.
Just as those seeds, when separated from the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, cannot sprout;
yet when they encounter the necessary conditions, the seed grows once more—so too, ignorance, karma, and craving must be abandoned;
one who abandons them is called a liberated one.
While these sentient beings of mine exist, there is no ultimate liberation.
Having abandoned the three [poisons] in every instance, they again obtain the three excellences;
because the self is ever-present, those [defilements] follow along in a subtle manner.
Because subtle faults persist, the mind is thus separated from skillful means.
Though you claim that long life is attained and that this is true liberation,
and though you say you have abandoned "mine," that which is abandoned does not exist.
Since the categories of existence are not separate [from the substance], how could the *guṇas* (qualities) be separate?
Therefore, as long as there are *guṇas*, one should know that it is not liberation.
*Guṇin* (the possessor of qualities) and *guṇa* (the quality) differ in meaning but are one in essence.
If one says they are separate, such a thing is ultimately impossible.
Heat cannot exist apart from fire; apart from fire, heat cannot be found.
It is like the space before the body: there is no "body-possessor" existing independently.
Thus, prior to the *guṇas*, there are no *guṇins*;
therefore, liberation occurs first, and only thereafter is there bondage to the body.
Furthermore, one knows that the cause is distinct from the body, whether it be conscious or unconscious.
If one says there is a knower, then there must be something known;
if there is something known, then it is not liberation.
If one says there is no knower, then I have nothing for which to strive.
If there were cognition apart from a self, then the self would be identical to wood or stone.
Fully knowing both the refined and the coarse, one turns away from the coarse and honors the subtle.
If one can relinquish everything, then all that is done will be ultimate.
Regarding the teachings of Ārāḍa, his mind could not find satisfaction;
knowing him to be no omniscient one, he should have proceeded further to seek what was superior.
He went to the seer Udraka, yet that one also maintained the notion of a self.
Though one contemplates subtle objects, one still perceives the faults of perception and non-perception.
Even abiding in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is no further path of escape;
for when sentient beings reach that state, they will inevitably fall back into regression.
Because the Bodhisattva sought liberation, he again abandoned the seer Udraka and further sought the supreme and wondrous path; he proceeded to Mount Gayāśīrṣa,
where the city was named the Forest of Asceticism (Duskaracaryā), and five bhikṣus were already dwelling there.
I saw those five bhikṣus, who had well-restrained their sensory faculties,
maintaining the precepts and practicing austerities while dwelling in that forest of asceticism by the banks of the Nairañjanā River—
a place of profound tranquility and great delight.
The Bodhisattva then remained there, contemplating in solitude in one place.
The five bhikṣus, knowing his intent to seek liberation with a focused mind,
served him with all their heart, honoring him as they would the god Īśvara.
Serving with humility, never departing from them in movement or stillness,
just as a practitioner’s faculties follow the lead of the mind;
the Bodhisattva, through diligent skillful means, shall deliver others from old age, sickness, and death.
He devoted himself single-mindedly to the practice of asceticism, restraining his body and forgetting to eat.
With a pure mind he observed the fasts and precepts, performing what others could not endure;
in silent meditation, he thus passed six years.
Eating but a single grain of sesame and rice daily, his body became utterly emaciated;
yet in seeking to cross over those who have not crossed, his heavy delusions only sank deeper.
The Path is accomplished through wisdom and understanding; abstaining from food is not its cause.
Though his four limbs were frail and weak, his wisdom-mind grew ever more radiant.
His spirit was serene and his body light;
his fame and virtue spread far and wide, like the waxing of the new moon or the blossoming of the kumuda flower.
Famous figures from across the land overflowed [to visit him], and men and women vied with one another to come and behold him.
His emaciated form was like a withered tree; thus six years were nearly complete.
Fearing the suffering of birth and death, he single-mindedly sought the cause of perfect enlightenment.
I reflected to myself: "It is not through this that the state of desirelessness and tranquil contemplation arises.
It is not as it was before, beneath the Jambu tree, when I attained that which was never before; know that that indeed is the Way."
The Way is not attained by a frail body; it must be sought through bodily effort.
When food and drink satisfy the sense-faculties, the faculties are gladdened and the mind becomes peaceful.
When the mind is peaceful, it accords with tranquility; such stillness serves as the means for meditative concentration.
Through meditation one knows the noble Dharma; by the power of the Dharma, that which is difficult to attain is attained.
Tranquil and free from old age and death, supreme and free from all defilements—such wondrous dharmas as these all arise from food and drink.
Having reflected on this meaning, he bathed at the Nairañjanā River;
having finished bathing and wishing to emerge from the pool, he was too weak and frail to rise.
A celestial deity pressed down a branch of a tree, and with his hand grasping it, he emerged.
At that time, by the side of that mountain forest, there was a cowherd chief whose eldest daughter was named Nanda.
A deity from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven came and told her:
"The Bodhisattva is in the woods; you should go and make offerings to him."
Nandapālaśa approached him with joy;
his hands were adorned with bracelets of white conch, and his body was clad in dyed blue robes.
The blue and white hues shone against one another, like pure water deep and vast.
With faith increasing and leaping with joy, he bowed his head at the Bodhisattva’s feet;
respectfully offering fragrant milk-rice, he prayed: "May you deign to accept it out of compassion.
The Bodhisattva accepted and ate it, whereby he attained the fruit of the present life.
Having eaten, his faculties were gladdened and he was fit to receive awakening.
His body was suffused with radiance, and his virtue and reputation grew ever more sublime—
like the ocean swelling with a hundred rivers, or like the new moon increasing in brightness day by day.
When the five bhikṣus saw him, they were startled and gave rise to feelings of disdain and wonder, thinking that his resolve for the Way had regressed;
they abandoned him and sought out a superior dwelling.
Like a person who has attained liberation, he was entirely detached from the five aggregates.
The Bodhisattva travels alone, Proceeding to that auspicious tree;
Beneath that very tree, He shall realize the path of perfect enlightenment.
That ground is vast, level, and even, Where soft, lush, and supple grasses grow.
With a peaceful and majestic gait like that of a lion, with every step the earth trembled.
The trembling of the earth moved the blind nāga, who, filled with joy, opened his eyes and saw clearly;
he spoke, saying, "I have seen former Buddhas, and the signs of the earth's trembling are just as they were then."
The Sage’s virtue is so profound that even the great earth cannot bear its weight;
with every step his feet tread upon the ground, a thunderous sound causes it to tremble.
A wondrous light illuminates the world beneath, as radiant as the morning sun.
A flock of five hundred bluebirds circled to the right, spiraling through the air;
a soft and cool breeze turned in accordance with their movement.
Such auspicious signs as these were entirely identical to those of the Buddhas of the past.
By this one knows that the Bodhisattva shall attain the path of perfect enlightenment.
From that grass-cutter, he obtained pure and soft grass;
having offered it beneath the tree, he sat upright and composed.
Sitting cross-legged without wavering, with his body coiled like a dragon,
he vowed not to rise from this seat until his task was fully accomplished.
Having made this true vow, the devas and nāgas were all filled with joy.
A cool, gentle breeze arises, yet the grasses and trees do not stir their branches;
all birds and beasts are hushed and utterly silent—
these are all signs that this Bodhisattva will surely attain the Way of Enlightenment.
The Great Seer of the royal lineage of seers, beneath the Bodhi tree,
established a firm vow to achieve the path of liberation.
The hosts of ghosts, nāgas, and devas were all filled with great joy.
The Dharma-enemy, the Heavenly King Māra, alone was sorrowful and displeased.
Sovereign over the five desires and possessing all martial arts, he detested and envied those seeking liberation; therefore, he is named Pāpīyān.
The Māra King has three daughters, Of beautiful appearance and graceful demeanor;
With various arts to delude men, They are the foremost among celestial maidens.
The first is named Desire-Stain, The next is named Able-to-Delight.
The three lovely daughters advanced together at once and said to their father, Pāpīyas:
"We do not know for what reason you are so sorrowful?"
The father related the matter in full, expressing his feelings to his daughters:
"In the world there is a Great Muni, clad in the great armor of vows,
wielding the great bow of the Self, with the sharp and keen arrows of wisdom."
Desiring to subdue sentient beings in battle, they shall destroy my realm.
If I am once defeated, sentient beings will place their faith in them;
all will return to the path of liberation, and my land will become empty and desolate.
Just as when a person violates the precepts, their body becomes empty and hollow;
so long as the eye of wisdom has not yet opened, my kingdom remains secure.
I shall go to destroy his resolve and cut off his bridge.
Grasping his bow and holding five arrows, accompanied by his male and female retinue,
he went to that Auspicious Forest (Kusinārā), wishing for the unease of all sentient beings. Seeing the Muni in silent composure,
intent on crossing the ocean of the three realms of existence, [he was struck with fear].
Holding a powerful bow in his left hand and drawing a sharp arrow with his right, he addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Death is truly terrifying; you must cultivate your own Dharma."
Abandoning the dharmas of liberation, one practices the battle of giving and merit;
by subduing all the world, one ultimately attains the bliss of rebirth in heaven.
This path is of excellent renown, practiced by the former victors.
The King of Seers is of the lineage of Gaozong; for a mendicant, this is not appropriate.
If you do not rise now, then settle your mind for a while;
be careful not to abandon your essential vow, and let me try discharging a single arrow.
Girika, the grandson of Candraprabha, was likewise struck by this arrow of mine;
though it touched him but slightly like a breeze, his mind fell into a state of madness.
Even the tranquil ascetics practicing austerities, upon hearing the sound of this arrow of mine, [were shaken].
The mind is seized by great terror, And in its confusion, it loses its true nature.
How much more so for you in this degenerate age— How can you hope to escape this arrow of mine?
If you rise up quickly now, You may yet attain safety.
This arrow’s poison is fierce; trembling with agitation, even one who deems themselves capable of enduring the arrow finds it difficult to remain at ease.
How much more so for you, who cannot endure the arrow—how could you not be struck with alarm?
When Māra spoke such words to intimidate the Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva’s mind remained serene; he neither doubted nor feared.
Māra the King then released his arrows and simultaneously sent forth three jade maidens.
The Bodhisattva did not look at the arrow, nor did he turn his gaze toward the three women;
the Māra-king was struck with alarm and doubt, and his heart and mouth spoke thus to one another:
"Once, as a woman of the Snowy Mountains, she shot at Maheśvara."
They may cause his mind to change, yet they cannot move the Bodhisattva.
Neither by these arrows nor by the three celestial jade maidens can his mind be shifted to give rise to desire or hatred.
He further gathered his military hosts, Coercing him with superior force.
While he was engaged in such reflections, The Māra army suddenly assembled;
Of various and diverse forms, They grasped halberds and wielded swords and blades.
Holding tridents and grasping golden pestles, they carry various implements of war.
With heads of pigs, fish, donkeys, and horses, and forms of camels, oxen, rhinoceroses, and tigers;
with heads of lions, dragons, and elephants, as well as other species of birds and beasts.
Some have a single body with many heads; some have one eye on each face, or else many eyes;
some have large bellies and long bodies;
some are emaciated and without bellies; some have long legs and large knees.
Some have large feet and thick calves; some have long fangs and sharp claws.
Some lack heads, eyes, or faces; some have two feet and many bodies.
Some have oversized or sideways faces; some appear the color of ash or dust.
Some resemble the light of a bright star; some emit smoke and fire from their bodies;
some carry mountains upon their elephant-like ears; some have disheveled hair and go naked;
some wear garments of leather; and the color of their faces is half red and half white.
Some wear garments of tiger skin, while others wear snake skins;
some have large bells girdled at their waists, while others wind their hair into spiral topknots;
some let their hair hang loose over their bodies, while others suck the vital essence from men.
Some take the lives of others; some leap and hurl themselves while crying out;
some run and pursue one another, repeatedly striking and harming each other;
some whirl in mid-air, while others fly and soar among the trees.
Some shrieked, huffed, and roared, their evil voices shaking heaven and earth.
Such various malevolent beings surrounded the Bodhi tree;
some sought to tear his body asunder, while others sought to devour him.
Fire blazes on all four sides, Its smoke and flames surge toward the heavens;
Mad winds rise up from every direction, And the mountains and forests tremble everywhere.
Wind, fire, smoke, and dust combine, Enveloping everything in darkness so that nothing can be seen.
The devas who love the Dharma, along with the nāgas, ghosts, and others, were all enraged at the host of Māra;
their eyes flowed with tears of indignation.
The assembly of devas from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, seeing Māra’s attempt to disturb the Bodhisattva, [were likewise moved].
Free from desire and without a mind of anger, he felt compassion and pity for them;
though all came to see the Bodhisattva, he sat upright, unmoving.
Surrounded by immeasurable Māras, their evil cries shook heaven and earth.
The Bodhisattva remains serene and silent, his radiant countenance showing no sign of change.
Like a lion king dwelling amidst the herd of beasts, all cry out in admiration: "Aha! Aha!"
How extraordinary and unprecedented!
The hosts of Māra urged one another on, each exerting his own power,
pressing and goading one another in turn, intending to crush and destroy him in an instant.
Tearing at their eyes and gnashing their teeth, they flew about in disorder and were utterly crushed.
The Bodhisattva observed them in silence, as if watching the play of children;
the various Māras grew even more enraged, doubling their strength for battle.
One who embraces a stone cannot lift it; one who has lifted it cannot set it down.
Flying spears, halberds, and sharp lances remain suspended in the void and do not fall.
Thunder rolls and great hailstones rain down, yet they transform into flowers of five colors.
Evil dragons and snakes spitting venom are transformed into fragrant breezes;
all manner of creatures who seek to harm the Bodhisattva cannot cause him to waver,
but instead bring injury upon themselves according to their own actions.
The Māra King had a sister named Mīghakālī;
holding a skull-bowl in her hand, she stood before the Bodhisattva and performed various strange gestures,
seeking to seduce and confuse him with lustful allurements.
Such hosts of Māras, with bodies of various hideous forms,
produced all manner of evil sounds, desiring to terrify the Bodhisattva;
yet they could not move even a single hair, and all the Māras were filled with grief and sorrow.
From the midst of the air, many deities bore him aloft; concealing their forms, they uttered these sounds:
"We have beheld the Great Muni, whose mind harbors no thought of resentment;
yet the evil and poisonous hearts of the various Māras give rise to enmity where there is no cause for it."
Foolish and evil Māras, you labor in vain and achieve nothing;
you should abandon your heart of malice and harm, and dwell in tranquil silence.
You cannot, with the breath from your mouth, blow and shake Mount Sumeru.
Fire is cold and water blazes; the nature of earth is level, soft, and supple.
These cannot destroy the Bodhisattva who has cultivated the fruits of goodness through kalpas.
With right reflection, the Bodhisattva applies himself with diligence and skillful means.
The light of pure wisdom shines upon all with compassion.
These four sublime virtues— how could they not be able to prevent interruption or obstruction,
so that the path to perfect enlightenment may be realized?
As the thousand rays of the sun inevitably dispel the darkness of the world,
as fire is obtained by drilling wood and water is found by digging the earth, so too,
through diligent and correct application of effort, there is nothing sought that cannot be attained.
The world has no protector; it is afflicted by the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, you seek the excellent medicine of wisdom to eliminate the suffering and afflictions of the world. Why then do you trouble and disturb me?
All those deluded and confused in the world are entirely attached to false paths;
the Bodhisattva practices the correct path, desiring to guide sentient beings.
To disturb and trouble the World-Honored Teacher would be utterly unacceptable.
Just as in a vast wilderness, when a merchant’s guide deceives them,
sentient beings fall into great darkness and know not where they are going;
for them, you have lit the lamp of wisdom— how can you wish to extinguish it?
All sentient beings are adrift and drowning In the great ocean of birth and death;
To serve as a boat of cultivated wisdom, How could you wish for them to sink?
Patience is the sprout of the Dharma, And firm resolve is the root of the Dharma.
The precepts of restraint are its roots, and right awakening its trunk;
this great tree of wisdom bears the fruit of the unsurpassed Dharma.
It provides shade and protection for all sentient beings—how can you wish to cut it down?
The shackles of greed, hatred, and delusion bind all sentient beings;
having practiced asceticism for long eons in order to untie these bonds, you have now definitively attained success. Here, you sit upon this true foundation.
Just as the Buddhas of the past, Firmly established their vajra pedestals,
While all other directions trembled, Only this ground remained secure.
Able to sustain the sublime meditative concentration, It cannot be destroyed by you.
One should simply humble the mind, eliminate all thoughts of pride and arrogance,
cultivate the perception of wisdom, and serve with patience.
When Māra heard the voice from the air and saw that the Bodhisattva remained serene and composed, he was struck with awe.
With shame and remorse, he abandoned pride and returned to the heavens by way of the path.
The hosts of Māra were all filled with grief and sorrow; their power and majesty crumbled away.
Their various weapons for battle were cast hither and thither, abandoned throughout the forests and wilds.
Just as when a man slays his enemy’s lord, The enemy’s faction is utterly crushed;
So now that the hordes of Māra have retreated and dispersed, The Bodhisattva’s mind is empty and still.
The radiance of the sun increases manifold, And all dust and mist are completely extinguished.
The moon shone bright and the many stars gleamed; once again, all darkness and obstructions vanished.
Heavenly flowers rained down from the sky as an offering to the Bodhisattva.
Having subdued the Māras, the Bodhisattva’s resolve was firm and his mind was at peace.
Seeking the exhaustion of ultimate truth, he entered profound and wondrous dhyāna.
With mastery over all samādhis, they appeared before him in succession;
entering meditative absorption during the first watch of the night, he recollected his past lives.
From such a place and with such a name, I have come to be born here;
In this way, hundreds of thousands, Of deaths and births, I fully know.
Experiencing immeasurable births and deaths, Among all classes of sentient beings,
All have once been my own kin, And thus I give rise to the mind of great compassion.
Having contemplated with this mind of great compassion,
I further observe those sentient beings wandering within the six realms of rebirth, Where birth and death are without end or limit.
Deceptive and lacking solidity, like a plantain tree, a dream, or an illusion—
at that very time of midnight, he attained the pure divine eye.
He beheld all sentient beings as if observing reflections in a mirror.
Sentient beings undergo birth and death, Whether noble or base, rich or poor.
Following pure or impure karma, They receive the retribution of suffering or joy;
Observe those who perform evil deeds— They shall be born within the evil realms.
Those who cultivate wholesome karma are born among humans and devas;
yet those born in the hells undergo immeasurable kinds of suffering:
they swallow and drink molten copper, and iron spears pierce their bodies.
Cast into boiling cauldrons of broth, driven into dense masses of fire;
devoured by packs of long-fanged dogs, pecked at the brain by sharp-beaked birds;
fearing the flames, they rush into the forest, where sword-leaves sever their bodies.
Sharp knives dissect their bodies, or sharp axes hack and chop them;
though they undergo such extreme suffering and poison, their karmic actions do not allow them to die.
Delighting in the cultivation of impure karma, they receive its retribution of extreme pain.
Attachment to flavors lasts but a moment, yet the retribution of suffering is exceedingly long.
One plants the causes of calamity through laughter and jesting, only to receive punishment amidst wailing and weeping.
If those sentient beings of evil karma could but see their own retribution!
The vital energies and channels will be severed; one will die in terror from hemorrhaging.
Having created various karmas of the animal realm, these karmas are diverse and distinct.
Upon death, one falls into the animal path, assuming various and distinct bodies.
Some die for their hides and flesh; for their hair, horns, bones, tails, and feathers.
They slaughter one another, and even kinsmen devour each other.
They carry heavy loads and bear the yoke, pricked by whips, goads, hooks, and needles.
Their bodies wounded, with pus and blood flowing, hunger and thirst cannot be relieved;
they turn upon one another in mutual slaughter, lacking any power of self-mastery.
Whether in the void, in water, or on land, there is nowhere to flee from death.
Those in whom stinginess and greed predominate are born in the realm of hungry ghosts;
their bodies are as massive as great mountains, yet the aperture of their throats is like the eye of a needle.
Blazing with the poisonous fire of hunger and thirst, they burn their own bodies from within.
Those who, when asked, are stingy and do not give, or who obstruct others from practicing generosity, will be born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). There they seek food but cannot obtain it;
they find only impure things discarded by people, which vanish as soon as they wish to eat them.
If a person hears that such is the bitter retribution for stinginess and greed,
they may cut their own flesh to give to others, like King Śibi;
yet others may be born among humans with bodies dwelling in a walking latrine.
Every movement brings extreme suffering; emerging from the womb gives rise to terror.
When the tender body touches external objects, it is as if being cut by swords and blades.
Subject to the portioning of one’s past karma, there is no time when death does not exist.
Striving with toil to seek birth, one obtains long life only to suffer further.
Those born in heaven by virtue of merit are constantly scorched by craving;
when their merit is exhausted and their lives end, the five signs of decay and death arrive.
Just as when tree blossoms wither, They become parched and lose their luster;
When kinsmen part from one another in life or death, The sorrow and suffering cannot be stayed.
The palace halls are vast and empty, And the jade maidens have all departed.
Sitting and lying in the dust, they weep with mutual longing;
those living grieve for their fall, while the dead yearn for life in sorrow.
Diligently practicing asceticism, they greedily seek the bliss of rebirth in heaven.
Since such suffering exists, how can one be so base as to crave it?
Even that which is obtained through great skillful means cannot avoid the pain of separation.
Alas, O devas and humans! Whether life be long or short, there is no difference in this regard.
Having practiced asceticism through accumulated kalpas, forever free from desire, they claimed to be eternally enduring;
yet now they have all fallen away.
They undergo manifold sufferings in hell, or as animals, they slaughter one another.
Hungry ghosts are oppressed by hunger and thirst; humans are exhausted by weariness and craving.
Though it is said that the gods possess bliss, the greatest suffering for them is separation.
Confused as they are born into this world, there is not a single place where one may find rest.
Alas! In the ocean of birth and death, The cycle of rebirth turns without end.
Sentient beings sink into the long current, Drifting and adrift with no place of refuge.
With such pure divine eyes, He observes the five realms of existence.
Deceptive and unstable, like a plantain tree, a bubble, or foam;
on that very third night, he entered into profound meditative absorption.
He observed all worlds as being of the nature of suffering within the cycle of saṃsāra.
Birth and death have occurred again and again, their number being beyond measure;
obscured by the darkness of craving and delusion, one knows not the way out.
With right mindfulness, contemplate within: from what do birth and death arise?
One definitively knows that old age and death are necessarily caused by birth;
just as when a person has a body, bodily pain follows.
Furthermore, one contemplates: what is the cause of birth?
I see that from the karma of various existences, the divine eye perceives these karmic existences;
they are not born of a sovereign creator, nor from self-nature, nor from a self, nor are they without cause.
Just as when the first knot of a bamboo is split, the remaining knots present no difficulty.
Having seen the cause of birth and death, one gradually perceives the reality:
that karma arises from grasping, just as fire finds fuel.
Grasping has craving as its cause, like a small fire consuming a mountain.
Knowing that craving arises from sensation, one perceives suffering and seeks pleasure and peace.
Just as hunger and thirst arise from the desire for food and drink, so too does craving arise from sensation.
With contact as its cause, the three types of sensation—suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure—are produced.
When the labor of drilling and kindling is applied, one obtains fire for use;
likewise, contact arises from the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), for the blind lack clear awakening.
The six sense bases arise from name-and-form (nāmarūpa), just as sprouts grow into stems and leaves.
Name-and-form arise from consciousness, just as sprouts and leaves grow from a seed;
consciousness in turn arises from name-and-form, revolving thus without end.
With consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, consciousness arises.
Just as a person and a boat advance together, with water and land mutually supporting their movement,
so consciousness gives rise to name-and-form, and name-and-form gives rise to the sense-faculties.
From the sense-faculties arises contact, and from contact, in turn, arises feeling.
Birth arises from craving; craving arises from grasping.
Grasping gives rise to karmic existence; existence gives rise to birth.
Birth gives rise to old age and death; thus the cycle of saṃsāra revolves without end.
The arising of sentient beings through causes and conditions, the Perfectly Awakened One fully awakens to;
having attained definitive perfect awakening, birth is ended and old age and death are extinguished.
With the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of grasping, existence ceases.
With the cessation of craving, grasping ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases.
With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases.
When all sense bases are extinguished, it is due to the cessation of name-and-form.
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases;
with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease. Thus the Great Seer achieves perfect awakening.
Having thus achieved perfect awakening, the Buddha arises in the world.
The Eightfold Path beginning with right view is a level and straight road;
ultimately free from the notion of "mine," it is like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
Having done what was to be done and attained the path of primordial perfect awakening, [the Tathāgata] has reached the end of suffering.
Having realized the ultimate primary truth, he entered the chamber of the Great Sage.
Darkness vanished and the light of wisdom arose; movement and stillness were entirely stilled in silence.
He attained the inexhaustible Dharma, and his omniscience shone with brilliant clarity.
The Great Sage’s virtue is profound and pure; the earth trembles everywhere, and the universe becomes entirely clear and bright.
Devas, nāgas, and spirits gather like clouds, and celestial music resounds in the sky as an offering to the Dharma.
A cool, refreshing breeze arises; though cloudless, a rain of fragrance falls.
Wondrous flowers bloom out of season, and sweet fruits ripen contrary to their natural time.
Great *maṇḍārava* flowers and various celestial jewel-blossoms appear.
Descending in disarray from the sky, they made offerings to the Honored Muni.
Sentient beings of various kinds all turned toward one another with hearts of loving-kindness;
their terrors were entirely dispelled, and they were free from all malice and arrogance.
All the worlds become as those whose outflows are exhausted;
the devas rejoice in liberation, the evil realms find temporary peace,
