A sprout grows because of a seed, yet the seed is not itself the sprout.
Neither identical nor different, so too is the birth of sentient beings.
The World-Honored One has spoken the truth, the equality of the ultimate meaning;
King Bimbisāra rejoiced, and the stainless Dharma-eye arose within him.
The king’s retinue and the people, along with hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities,
having heard the teaching of the nectar-like Dharma, likewise followed him in leaving behind all defilements.
At that time, King Bimbisāra bowed his head and entreated the World-Honored One:
He moved his residence to the Bamboo Grove;
out of compassion for those he had loved, he remained silent.
Having already seen the Truths, the King paid his respects and returned to the palace.
The World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, moved his residence to the peaceful Bamboo Grove.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, he established the bright lamp of wisdom,
dwelling in the Brahma-abodes, the celestial abodes, and the abodes of the noble sages.
At that time, Aśvajit, having disciplined his mind and governed his sense faculties,
went forth at the proper hour to beg for food and entered the city of Rājagṛha.
His appearance was preeminent in the world, and his deportment was composed, orderly, and dignified.
The men and women within the city, upon seeing him, were all filled with joy;
those walking stopped in their tracks, while those ahead came forward to welcome him and those behind followed as swiftly as the wind.
The Seer Kapila extensively delivered his many disciples.
The foremost among those of great learning, whose name was Śāriputra,
saw a bhikṣu proceeding with dignified composure, his faculties serene and tranquil.
Pausing on the path and waiting for him to arrive, he raised his hand and asked:
“Your youthful and serene countenance is something I have never seen before.
What sublime and wondrous Dharma have you attained?
Whom do you take as your teacher?”
"What does the Teacher’s teaching proclaim?
I pray you will resolve my doubts.
The bhikṣu, delighted by his question, replied with a serene countenance and humble words:
"Endowed with all-knowledge, born of the noble Ikṣvāku lineage,
the most honored among gods and humans— he is my Great Teacher. As for me,
my years are yet young and my days of study are but recently begun."
How could I possibly proclaim the Great Master’s most profound and subtle meaning?
Now, with my shallow intelligence, I shall briefly explain the Teacher’s doctrine:
all phenomena that arise are born entirely from causes and conditions.
When all phenomena of arising and ceasing are extinguished, it is said that the Way serves as the skillful means.
For the two, Upatiṣya and Kolita, as they listened, their minds merged in harmony;
far removed from all dust and defilement, the pure Dharma-eye arose.
Previously, in my fixed convictions, I held that causes and non-causes were known;
I thought all things were uncreated and entirely dependent upon the Sovereign Lord (Īśvara).
Now, having heard the Dharma of Dependent Origination, the wisdom of selflessness has been opened and clarified.
The various subtle afflictions increase; none are able to eliminate them completely.
Only the teaching of the Tathāgata exhausts them forever without remainder.
By not grasping at "what belongs to me," one is able to transcend the self.
When the lamp of the sun rises, who can cause its light to vanish?
Though one may sever the stalk of a lotus, its fine fibers remain continuous;
yet when the Buddha’s teaching removes afflictions, it is like cutting through stone, leaving nothing behind.
He paid homage at the feet of the bhikṣu, took his leave, and returned home;
the bhikṣu, having finished his alms-round, likewise returned to the Bamboo Grove.
When Śāriputra returned home, his countenance was exceedingly serene and refined.
The virtuous friend Mahāmaudgalyāyana, equal to him in realization and learning,
saw Śāriputra from afar with a most joyful countenance and said:
“Now that I behold you, you possess an extraordinary countenance; though your natural disposition was ever profoundly reserved, today we meet with joy.
You must have attained the Dharma of Ambrosia, for this sign cannot be without cause.”
He replied: "The Tathāgata has told me that I have truly attained an unprecedented Dharma.
He immediately requested that he preach it for me; upon hearing it, my mind was opened and liberated."
All defilements were likewise removed, and the eye of the True Dharma arose accordingly.
Having long cultivated sublime causes and effects, as clearly as seeing a lamp in the palm of one's hand,
they attained unshakable faith in the Buddha and together proceeded to where the Buddha was.
Together with his retinue of two hundred and fifty disciples,
the Buddha saw the two worthies from afar and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Those two who are coming are my foremost disciples."
First, his wisdom is peerless; second, his supernormal powers are foremost.
With a profound and pure Brahma-voice, he immediately commanded you, "Welcome!
Herein lies the Dharma of cool serenity, the ultimate path for leaving the household life."
Holding a triple-pronged staff, with matted hair and carrying a water jar,
upon hearing the Buddha’s voice of welcome, “Come, well-come,” he immediately transformed into a śramaṇa.
Both masters and disciple all assumed the deportment of bhikṣus.
They bowed their heads at the feet of the World-Honored One and withdrew to sit on one side;
as he preached the Dharma to them in accordance with their needs, they all attained the path of Arhatship.
At that time, there were two beings, the bright lamps of the Kāśyapa clan.
Possessing great learning and endowed with auspicious physical marks, his wealth was abundant and his wife most virtuous;
yet he renounced them all to leave the home-life, vowing to seek the path of liberation.
On the road, passing by the Cāpāla Shrine, he suddenly encountered Śākyamuni.
His radiant countenance was brilliantly manifest, like a banner raised for a celestial sacrifice.
With solemn reverence, he raised his entire body in worship and prostrated himself at the feet [of the Buddha], saying:
"The Venerable One is my Great Teacher; I am the Venerable One’s disciple."
Having long accumulated the darkness of ignorance, I pray that you will act as a lamp of light for me.
The Buddha, knowing the inclinations of those two beings who delighted in the pursuit of liberation,
addressed them with a pure and gentle voice, saying, "Come, welcome."
Hearing these instructions, my mind became harmonious and serene; the exhaustion of body and spirit was stilled.
My heart dwells in supreme liberation, tranquil and free from all defilements.
Out of great compassion, according to what is appropriate, I have briefly explained this for you.
Having realized all profound dharmas and attained the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence, his great virtue spread everywhere; therefore, he was named Mahākāśyapa.
Originally he viewed the body and the self as distinct, or else he viewed the self as being identical to the body.
The views of "I" and "mine" have been forever eradicated;
one sees only this mass of suffering, and beyond the cessation of suffering, nothing remains.
To maintain precepts and practice asceticism while regarding them as the cause [of liberation] when they are not the cause—this is a mistaken view.
Seeing the nature of suffering with equanimity, one is forever free from the mind that clings to other aggregates.
Whether existence or non-existence is perceived, the two views give rise to hesitation;
but seeing the true reality with equanimity, one becomes certain and free from further doubt.
Attached to wealth and form, one becomes intoxicated by the arising of craving;
through the perception of impermanence and impurity, greedy attachment is forever brought to an end.
With a mind of loving-kindness and equanimity, one holds no distinction between enemy and kin.
By feeling compassion for all beings, one eliminates the poison of anger.
Based on forms, various perceptions of resistance arise;
by contemplating the dissolution of the perception of form, one severs craving for form.
Though one be born among the gods of the formless realm, life must inevitably come to an end;
the fool, regarding the four meditative attainments, conceives the notion of liberation.
Yet true quiescence is the departure from all perceptions, wherein craving for the formless is forever eliminated.
The agitated mind is turbulent and contrary, like wild winds churning the waves;
by entering deeply into firm concentration, one stills the restless and distracted mind.
Contemplating that all phenomena are without "mine" and that arising and ceasing are not solid, [one realizes their instability].
Not perceiving the inferior, the middling, or the superior, the mind of self-conceit naturally vanishes.
Kindling the lamp of wisdom, one leaves behind all the darkness of delusion;
seeing the dharma of exhaustion and non-exhaustion, ignorance is entirely eliminated without remainder.
Contemplating the ten virtues, the ten kinds of afflictions are extinguished;
having attained rest and fulfilled what was to be done, I feel deep gratitude and look up to your venerable countenance.
Having abandoned the three and attained the three, the three disciples have eliminated the three.
Like the three stars arrayed in the sky, the thirty-three deities attend upon the Three and Five;
likewise, the three attendants serve the Buddha.
At that time, there was a great elder named Anāthapiṇḍada.
Possessing immense wealth and immeasurable riches, he practiced extensive giving to relieve the poor and destitute.
Having traveled from afar from the north, from the kingdom of Kośala,
he stayed at the house of a friend whose name was Śūra.
Hearing that the Buddha had appeared in the world and was dwelling nearby at the Bamboo Grove, he honored his reputation and esteemed his virtue; thus, that very night, he went to that grove.
The Tathāgata already knew him: his faculties were mature and pure faith had arisen.
In accordance with what is appropriate and in accord with reality, he spoke these words of Dharma:
"Since you have delighted in the True Dharma and possess a pure faith that thirsts for it,
you have been able to diminish your sleep and have come to pay me respectful homage."
Today, for your sake, I shall provide you with the full rites of a guest of honor.
Because you have planted roots of virtue in the past, your aspirations are firm and pure;
hearing the name of the Buddha, you rejoice and are fit to be a vessel for the True Dharma.
With an open mind, he practiced extensive acts of kindness, providing for the poor and destitute;
his fame and virtue spread everywhere, a fruit brought about by past causes.
Now he shall practice the gift of Dharma, bestowing it with a sincere and devoted heart.
At that time, one bestows the gift of tranquility, while simultaneously upholding the pure precepts.
Precepts serve as ornaments; they can turn one away from evil realms, cause one to ascend to heaven, and reward one with the five celestial pleasures.
All seeking brings great suffering; desire accumulates all faults.
One should practice the avoidance of evil; the bliss of detachment is tranquility.
Knowing the suffering of old age, illness, and death as the world’s greatest affliction, [one should seek liberation].
Observing the world correctly, one becomes free from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Having seen that among human beings there is the suffering of old age, sickness, and death, one sees that it is likewise for those born in the heavens; there is nothing that exists eternally.
What is impermanent is suffering; where there is suffering, there is no self.
Since it is impermanent, suffering, and not-self, how can there be "I" or "mine"?
To know that suffering is indeed suffering, and that its origin is indeed its origin—
The cessation of suffering is tranquility; the Path is the place of peace.
The nature of sentient beings is one of flux; know this to be the root of suffering.
By wearying of the branches and blocking the source, one no longer desires existence or non-existence.
The fierce fires of birth, old age, and death blaze everywhere throughout the world;
seeing the agitation of birth and death, one should practice signlessness (animitta).
This is the ultimate samādhi, the nectar-like state of tranquility.
Empty and devoid of self or what belongs to a self, the world is entirely like an illusion;
one should contemplate this body as a mere collection of the activities of the great elements.
Upon hearing this teaching, the elder immediately attained the first fruit.
The ocean of birth and death has been extinguished, leaving only a single drop remaining.
Though one may dwell in seclusion practicing detachment and attain the formless state of the Peak of Existence,
it is not equal to a worldly person today who perceives the Truth and attains true liberation.
Not free from various ascetic practices and the web of diverse views,
though they reach the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), they do not perceive the true meaning.
With false conceptions fixated on celestial blessings, their bonds of craving become ever deeper.
When the elder heard the teaching of the Dharma, his hindrances and obscurations were suddenly cleared away;
he attained right view, and all false views were forever eliminated,
just as a fierce autumn wind scatters thick clouds.
The world is not produced by a cause of sovereign power, nor does it arise from a false cause,
nor indeed from no cause at all. If it were born from a creator god,
there would be no distinction between old and young, nor priority and sequence.
Furthermore, there is no wheel of the five destinies; those who are born should not perish.
There should be no calamities or afflictions, and committing evil would not be a transgression;
both pure and impure karma are caused by the Lord Maheśvara.
If the world were born from Īśvara, there should be no doubt;
just as a son is born from a father, who would not recognize his own kin?
When a person encounters poverty and suffering, they should not, in turn, resent Heaven.
One should revere only Īśvara and not worship other deities.
If Īśvara were the creator, he could not be called "Īśvara" (the Sovereign),
because since he is a maker, he would have to be constantly making.
If one acts constantly, one tires oneself; how can this be called mastery?
If one acts without a deliberate mind, it is like the behavior of an infant;
if one acts with a deliberate mind, having such a mind is not mastery.
Since suffering and pleasure arise from sentient beings, they are not created by Īśvara.
If Īśvara produced suffering and pleasure, he would necessarily possess love and hatred;
because he would already possess love and hatred, he should not be called "Īśvara."
If, moreover, [the world] were created by an *īśvara*, sentient beings should remain silent;
left to the power of that *īśvara*, what need would there be to cultivate goodness?
Even if one were to cultivate good or evil, there should be no karmic retribution.
If Īśvara were born of karma, then everything would be a product of collective karma.
If everything were a product of collective karma, then all should be called Īśvara.
If Īśvara were without a cause, then everything else should likewise be non-existent.
If [the Lord] were caused by another Lord, there would be an infinite regress of Lords;
therefore, all sentient beings are entirely without a creator.
One should know that the doctrine of a Lord is thus refuted in this treatise.
All meanings would be contradictory; if there were no teaching, there would be fault.
If things were produced from their own intrinsic nature, the fault would likewise be the same.
Those who are learned in logic have never asserted such a thing.
Without dependence and without cause, nothing can be produced;
all things arise from causes, just as they depend upon seeds.
Therefore, know that everything does not arise through its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
All things that are produced do not arise from a single cause alone;
yet you speak of a single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, that [nature] is not a cause.
If you say that this intrinsic nature pervades all places, [it would follow that it is not a productive cause].
If it were omnipresent, there would be neither agent nor action;
since there is neither agent nor action, it could not be a cause.
If it pervaded all places, then everything would have an agent.
In that case, at all times, there would always be something being produced.
If one says that production occurs eternally, then things would not depend on time for their arising.
Therefore, one should know that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be the cause.
Furthermore, it is said that its intrinsic nature is devoid of all *guṇas* (qualities);
likewise, all performed actions should also be devoid of *guṇas*.
Yet, throughout all the worlds, everyone perceives the existence of *guṇas*.
Therefore, know that intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is likewise not a cause.
If one asserts that this intrinsic nature is distinct from its qualities (guṇa),
then because it is held to be eternal as the cause, its nature ought not to be different [from them].
Because the qualities (*guṇa*) of sentient beings differ, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be their cause.
If intrinsic nature were eternal, then phenomena would likewise not undergo destruction.
Since intrinsic nature is posited as the cause, the principle of cause and effect ought to be identical.
Because the world is seen to undergo destruction, one should know that there must be a distinct cause for this.
If its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were the cause, liberation could not be sought;
since an intrinsic nature would exist, it would simply have to endure its own arising and ceasing.
Even if one were to attain liberation, the intrinsic nature would still give rise to bondage.
If the non-perception of intrinsic nature were the cause for seeing the Dharma,
it too could not be the cause, because the principles of cause and effect are distinct.
Regarding all phenomena of worldly views, both cause and effect are fully perceived.
If intrinsic nature were devoid of mind, there could be no causal factor for mind;
just as one knows fire by seeing smoke, one seeks the characteristics of cause and effect through their mutual correspondence.
It is not that because their cause is unseen, A perceived phenomenon arises;
just as vessels and garments are fashioned from gold, From beginning to end they do not depart from gold.
The self-nature is the cause of the phenomenon; How could it differ from beginning to end?
If time were the agent of action, one should not seek liberation;
for since that time is eternal, one would have to submit to its seasons.
The world would be without end, and time likewise would be so.
Therefore, the practitioner should not seek through expedient means the categories of substance (dravya) and quality (guṇa),
nor the worldly debates on identity and difference;
though there are various such explanations, one should know that they do not have a single cause.
If it were said that the self is the agent, it should arise according to one's desire;
yet now it does not follow desire—how then can it be said that the self acts?
What is undesired is obtained, while what is desired is instead contradicted.
Suffering and pleasure are not under one's own control; how can one say "I am the doer"?
If I were the creator, there would be no karma for the miserable realms;
yet various karmic fruits arise—therefore, know that it is not I who act.
To say, "I act according to time," implies that at such a time one should only perform good;
yet good and evil arise according to conditions, so we know it is not "I" who acts.
If things were produced without cause, there would be no need to cultivate skillful means.
If all things were spontaneous and fixed, for what purpose would one cultivate causes?
Since various worldly karmas yield various fruits,
we know that nothing is produced without a cause.
Whether with mind or without mind, all arise from causes and conditions;
no phenomenon in the world is born without a cause.
The elder’s mind was opened and liberated, as he thoroughly penetrated this supreme and wondrous meaning.
The wisdom of the single mark of reality having arisen, he definitively realized the ultimate truth.
Bowing at the feet of the World-Honored One, he joined his palms and made this request:
"Residing in Śrāvastī, the land is abundant, peaceful, and blissful."
Great King Prasenajit, of the noble lineage of Siṃhahanu,
whose merit and fame spread afar and who is revered by those near and far,
desires to construct a vihāra; we pray only that you will compassionately accept it.
Knowing the Buddha’s mind to be impartial, he does not seek comfort in his dwelling;
out of compassion for those sentient beings, he did not reject my request.
The Buddha, knowing the elder’s heart, has now undertaken this great act of giving.
Untainted and unattached, you skillfully protect the minds of sentient beings.
You have already seen the True Dharma; your original heart delights in practicing generosity.
Wealth is not a permanent treasure; you ought to practice giving swiftly.
Just as when a storehouse is set ablaze, those who have already emerged are safe;
so too, the wise person, knowing impermanence, brings forth wealth and practices generosity extensively.
The stingy and greedy guard their hoards with parsimony, fearing they will be exhausted and thus refusing to enjoy them.
Nor do they fear impermanence; to lose [the opportunity] in vain only increases sorrow and regret.
Giving at the proper time and to a worthy recipient is like a valiant man facing the enemy;
one who can both give and fight is a hero of wisdom.
The giver is beloved by the multitude; their good reputation spreads far and wide.
The virtuous delight in being their friend, and at the end of life, their mind remains ever joyful.
Free from regret and free from fear, they are not reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts.
This is but the floral retribution; its fruit is inconceivable.
Amidst the wandering through the six realms, there is no better companion than giving.
If one is born among gods or humans, one will be honored and served by all.
Born into the realm of animals, one experiences the joy that follows as the fruit of giving;
through wisdom, one cultivates tranquility and concentration, becoming independent and beyond measure.
Though one may attain the path of the Deathless, it is still sustained and perfected by the merit of giving.
By virtue of that act of giving, one cultivates the eight recollections of a great person.
With a mind full of joy through these recollections, one attains decisive samādhi;
as concentration increases wisdom, one is able to correctly contemplate arising and ceasing.
Having correctly contemplated arising and ceasing, one attains liberation in succession.
One who gives away wealth in charity eliminates greedy attachment;
by bestowing with compassion and reverence, one simultaneously removes envy, anger, and pride.
Clearly seeing the fruit of giving, one eliminates the deluded view of non-giving;
all fetters and afflictions are extinguished—this is due to the practice of giving.
One should know that the giver of gifts is the cause of liberation.
Just as a person plants a tree for the sake of shade, flowers, and fruit, so too is giving: it yields the joy of the great nirvana.
By giving wealth that is not firm, one obtains the fruit of a firm reward.
By giving food, one gains strength; by giving clothing, one attains a beautiful complexion.
If one establishes a monastery, all fruits will be fully realized.
Whether giving with the hope of seeking the five desires, or out of greed for great wealth—
Some give for the sake of fame; some seek the joy of rebirth in heaven, or give to escape the suffering of poverty.
Among all forms of giving, there is none that does not yield its benefit.
Whatever your mind aspires to accomplish, may it be swiftly fulfilled.
When the deluded and craving heart departs, the eye of purity shall open once more.
Having received the Buddha’s teaching, the elder’s compassionate mind grew ever more luminous.
He invited Upatiṣya, his virtuous friend with whom he returned to Kośala;
traveling about, they sought an auspicious site.
There they beheld Prince Jeta’s Grove, where the woods and streams were most serene and secluded.
He went to where the Prince was and requested to purchase his field.
The Prince cherished it most dearly and had no intention at all to sell it, saying:
"Even if you were to spread gold over it until it was full, I would still not part with this land."
The elder’s heart was filled with joy, and he immediately spread the gold everywhere.
Jeta said, "I will not give it; how can you spread the gold?
The elder said, "I have not given it; why do you say it is covered in gold?"
The two men disputed together, and the dispute extended even to the judge.
The multitude all marveled at this marvel, and Jeta also recognized their sincerity;
he inquired extensively into the causes and conditions, and they spoke of establishing a vihāra.
He made offerings to the Tathāgata, as well as to the community of bhikṣus.
Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, the Crown Prince’s mind was immediately awakened;
he took only half of the gold and sought to join with others to establish [the shrine].
“Your land and my grove, let us together offer them to the Buddha.
The householder gave his land and the deity his grove to Śāriputra;
there the monastery was begun and, through diligent effort day and night, it was swiftly completed.
Exalted, magnificent, and most splendidly adorned, It was like the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings.
In accordance with the Dharma and suited to the Way, It was worthy of the Tathāgata;
such as had never existed before in the world, It increased the splendor of the city of Śrāvastī.
The Tathāgata manifested his divine protection, and the assembly of sages gathered for the rains retreat.
For those without attendants, he compassionately descended; for those with attendants, it was fitting for their path to the Way.
By virtue of this merit, the elder, when his life ended, ascended to heaven.
His descendants succeeded to his legacy, planting fields of merit through successive generations.
In the kingdom of Magadha, the Buddha transformed all manner of heterodox paths,
bringing them all to the single flavor of the Dharma, like the sun outshining the host of stars.
Emerging from that city of Pañcāla, accompanied by a thousand disciples and followed by his retinue of attendants before and behind, he proceeded toward Mount Nyiṅka.
Near Kapilavastu, he gave rise to a heart of gratitude.
While performing the ritual offerings, he served his father, the King.
The royal preceptor and the great ministers first dispatched attendants to constantly follow him on his left and right, observing his every movement.
Knowing that the Buddha wished to return to his kingdom, [the charioteer] hurried ahead and reported:
"The Prince went far away to study; now that his vows are fulfilled, he has returned.
Upon hearing this, the King was filled with great joy; he prepared his carriage and immediately went out to welcome him.
All the officials and commoners of the entire kingdom followed the king.
As they drew near, they saw the Buddha from afar; his radiant marks were twice as magnificent as his former appearance.
Standing amidst the great assembly, he was like the Brahma King.
Descending from the carriage, he advanced slowly, fearing that the Dharma might present obstacles;
beholding his countenance, he rejoiced inwardly, yet his mouth knew not what to say.
He looked back at his own lingering attachment to worldly burdens, while his son had transcended to ascend as an immortal.
Although you dwell in the honored Way, we do not yet know what name you bear.
Reflecting upon myself, I have long been parched with thirst, yet today there was no way to express it;
you now sit in silence, peaceful and with an unaltered countenance.
Long parted from you, my feelings have grown cold, leaving my heart alone in sorrow;
like a man long parched with thirst who encounters a clear, cool spring on his way,
he rushes forward eager to drink, only to find the spring suddenly dried up at the moment he reaches it.
Now that I behold my son, his countenance is still that same radiant glow.
His mind is distant and his spirit loftily transcendent; he has no heart for the protection of kin.
He suppresses his emotions and severs all vain hopes, like one who thirsts before a dried-up spring.
Before seeing her, my proliferating thoughts ran wild; facing her now, there is no joy.
It is like a man who, longing for his kin, suddenly beholds a painted likeness.
Worthy to rule over the four continents, he is just like King Mandhātṛ.
As you now go forth to beg for alms, how can this path bring you true honor?
Your tranquility is like Mount Sumeru; your radiant marks are as bright as the sun.
You walk with the measured gait of a bull king and roar the fearless lion’s roar.
He did not accept the offerings of the four kings, but sustained his body by begging for alms.
The Buddha, knowing that his father the king’s heart still harbored the thought of him as a son,
opened the king’s mind and, out of compassion for all beings, [taught him].
Rising into the void by means of the bases of supernormal power, holding the sun and moon in both hands,
he wanders through the air, performing various miraculous transformations;
sometimes dividing his body into countless forms, and then again merging them back into one.
Sometimes he enters water as if it were earth; sometimes he enters earth as if it were water.
Stone walls do not obstruct his body, and from his left and right sides, he emits water and fire.
The father king was greatly delighted, and the bonds of affection between father and son were entirely severed.
From a lotus seat in the air, [the Buddha] preached the Dharma to the King:
"I know that your heart is filled with compassionate concern, Increasing your grief and sorrow for your son;
Bound by deep affection for your child, You ought to quickly extinguish it."
Calm his mind by ceasing craving and receive from me the training of a son—
what no other son has ever offered, I now offer to you, Father King.
What you have not yet received from a son, you shall now receive from me, your son.
The marvels of a human king are extraordinary, and those of a celestial king are likewise rare;
this most excellent path of ambrosia I now offer to the Great King.
Through one's own karma one undergoes birth; karma is the basis for the retribution of karma.
One should know the causes and effects of karma; diligently practice the deeds that transcend the world.
Contemplating the world with clarity, one finds that karma alone is a true friend.
Even toward relatives and one's own body, though there be deep affection and longing—
At the end of life, the spirit departs alone; only karma follows as a true companion.
Wandering through the five realms of existence, birth occurs in three ways according to the three types of karma.
Craving and desire act as its cause, resulting in the various distinctions among different species.
Now I shall exert all my strength, purifying the karma of body and speech;
practicing diligently day and night, I shall stifle the distracted mind until it is tranquil.
Only this is my own true benefit; apart from this, nothing is mine at all.
Know that the existence within the three realms is like the surging waves of the sea;
it is difficult to find joy in and difficult to associate with. One should cultivate the fourth type of action;
the wheel of birth and death in the five destinies revolves like the many stars.
Even the gods are subject to change; how could those among humans remain constant?
Nirvana is the supreme peace, and meditative stillness is the best among pleasures.
The five sensual pleasures of a human king are perilous and full of terror.
Like dwelling together with a venomous snake, how could there be even a moment’s joy?
When the wise person views the world as being surrounded by a blazing fire,
they are terrified and find no temporary peace, seeking only liberation from birth, old age, and death.
The place of inexhaustible tranquility is where the wise dwell;
they require no sharp weapons, nor elephants, horses, or war chariots.
By subduing greed, hatred, and delusion, they are invincible against any foe in the world.
Knowing suffering and severing its cause, realizing cessation and cultivating the means—
having perfectly awakened to the Four Noble Truths, the terrors of the evil realms were removed.
First manifesting wondrous supernormal powers, he caused the king’s heart to rejoice.
Their faith and devotion having deepened, they became fit vessels for the True Dharma;
with palms joined, they praised him:
"How marvelous! Your vow has borne fruit; how marvelous! You have freed us from great suffering; how marvelous! You have brought us such benefit!"
Although my sorrow and grief first increased, through that very grief I have gained this benefit.
How marvelous! Today, for me, the fruition of having borne a son has been realized.
It is fitting to renounce superior and exquisite pleasures; it is fitting to apply oneself with diligence to what is difficult.
You should leave behind the glory of your kin; you should sever the bonds of affection and love.
The various royal sages of antiquity labored in vain without merit, yet you have now fully attained that place of coolness and tranquility.
Establishing myself in peace, I bring peace to others; with great compassion, I rescue all sentient beings.
Formerly, when you dwelt in the world as a Wheel-Turning King, it was through your sovereign supernormal powers that you caused my mind to open and be liberated.
Nor was there this sublime Dharma that brings me joy today.
Had I been a Wheel-Turning King, the threads of birth and death would not have been severed;
now that birth and death are ended, the great suffering of saṃsāra has been extinguished.
For the sake of all classes of sentient beings, you extensively preach the Dharma of ambrosia.
With such wondrous supernormal powers and wisdom so profound and vast,
you have forever extinguished the suffering of birth and death, becoming the supreme among devas and humans.
Though he occupied the throne of a holy king, he ultimately did not obtain such benefit.
Having praised him in this way, his love for the Dharma increased and his reverence grew;
though he sat in the honored position of a royal father, he humbly bowed his head in salutation.
The people within the kingdom, beholding the Buddha’s supernatural powers and hearing him preach the profound and wondrous Dharma, as well as seeing the King’s reverence,
joined their palms and prostrated with their heads at his feet; they all conceived thoughts of extraordinary wonder.
Weary of the burdens of worldly life, they all gave rise to the mind of renunciation.
The various princes of the Śākya clan, having awakened to the realization of the fruits of the Path,
all grew weary of worldly glory and pleasure, forsaking their kin and loved ones to leave the home life.
Ānanda and Nanda, Kapphiṇa and Anuruddha,
Upananda and Khaṇḍadravya, as well as Kumārakassapa—
these and other preeminent leaders among the Śākya clansmen.
All followed the Buddha’s teaching, receiving the Dharma as his disciples.
The sons of high ministers who governed the state, with Udāyin at their head,
together with all the princes, went forth into homelessness in successive order.
Furthermore, the Ācārya named Upāli,
seeing those princes and the sons of ministers who had left the household life,
felt his heart open with emotion and likewise received the dharma of renunciation.
When the Father King beheld his son’s supernormal powers and various merits,
he himself entered the pure stream of the nectar-like gateway of the True Dharma.
Renouncing the royal throne and the kingdom, he entrusted them to Amṛtodana.
Dwelling in seclusion, he cultivated silence; residing in the palace, he practiced the way of the royal sages.
The Tathāgata fully guided and converted him; once his kinsmen and acquaintances were won over, his countenance was serene and joyful amidst the path, and his relatives followed him with delight.
When the time arrived for him to beg for alms, he entered Kapilavastu;
the men and women of the city were filled with wonder and joy, raising their voices in song:
"Siddhārtha Ārāḍa has returned, having completed his study of the Way!"
Those inside and outside hurriedly informed one another; great and small alike rushed out to look.
From within the gates and windows, they pressed shoulder to shoulder, casting sidelong glances.
They beheld the Buddha’s body with its excellent marks and signs, its radiance exceedingly brilliant and resplendent.
Externally he wears the kashaya robe, while his inner bodily radiance shines through;
like the orb of the sun, the interior and exterior reflect one another.
Those who behold him feel both sorrow and joy in their hearts, joining their palms as tears flow down.
Beholding the Buddha’s measured and dignified gait, he restrained his physical form and gathered his senses;
the wondrous body manifested the Dharma-dignity, increasing his reverence, his sense of loss, and his sighs of lamentation.
His hair was shorn and his fine appearance altered, his body clad in dyed robes.
With such majestic bearing and refined countenance, you walk with body restrained and eyes fixed upon the ground.
You ought to wear a precious canopy of feathers and grasp the reins of the flying dragon;
why instead do you expose yourself to drifting dust, holding an alms bowl to beg for food?
Your skill is sufficient to subdue enemies; your appearance is enough to delight the court ladies.
Adorned in splendid robes and a celestial crown, the common people all look up toward you with reverence.
Why then do you constrain your noble countenance, binding your mind and restraining your form?
Having renounced exquisite desires, fine garments, and radiant robes, you wear a simple body clad in dyed saffron cloth.
What vision do you see, and what do you seek, that you abandon the five worldly sensual pleasures, which are but enemies?
Having forsaken your virtuous wife and beloved son, you delight in solitude and wander alone.
How difficult it was for that virtuous consort, who through the long night harbored sorrowful thoughts!
Now that she has heard of his renunciation, her very life is preserved;
yet I do not know whether King Śuddhodana will ever again behold this son.
Beholding his wondrous physical form, he has discarded his appearance to leave the household;
even an enemy would feel pained and regretful at this—how could his father remain at ease upon seeing him?
His beloved son Rāhula constantly weeps with sorrowful longing.
Seeing no heart of consolation, for what purpose do you study this path?
Those who are skilled in the signs of the marks all say that the Prince was born endowed with the marks of a Great Man;
he ought to enjoy the sovereignty over the four seas.
Observing what is done now, all of this is but empty talk;
many such as these abound, speaking with confusion and disorder.
The Tathāgata’s mind is free from attachment; he feels neither joy nor sorrow.
Out of compassion and pity for sentient beings, desiring to free them from the suffering of poverty,
he increases their roots of goodness for the sake of future lives as well.
He manifests the traces of few desires and simultaneously removes the slanders of worldly dust.
Entering the poor quarters to beg for alms, accepting whatever is obtained, whether coarse or refined,
and not discriminating between great or small households, he returns with his bowl full to the mountain forests.
The World-Honored One has already transformed and enlightened the people of Kapilavastu.
Having completed his work of saving beings according to conditions,
he traveled together with the great assembly toward the kingdom of Kośala to visit King Prasenajit.
Jetavana had already been adorned, and the halls and residences were all fully prepared.
Flowing springs pour into one another, and flowers and fruits all flourish in splendor;
various wondrous birds of land and water warble in harmony according to their kind.
Possessing every beauty beyond compare in the world, it is like the palace on Mount Kailāsa.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, with his retinue, sought out the path to welcome him;
scattering flowers and burning famous incense, he invited him to enter the Jetavana.
Holding a golden dragon pitcher in his hand, he knelt in person to pour forth a stream of long water.
With this Jetavana Monastery, I offer as a gift to the Sangha of the ten directions.
May the World-Honored One accept it with his blessing, stabilizing the nation and ensuring its long-term peace.
For the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada, may blessings and prosperity flow forth without end.
At that time, King Prasenajit, hearing that the World-Honored One had arrived,
prepared his carriage and went out from the Jetavana Grove. He paid homage at the feet of the World-Honored One,
withdrew to sit to one side, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I never imagined that this lowly, small kingdom would suddenly attain such great auspiciousness;
though the wicked and rebellious have brought much calamity, how could they have moved a Great Man?
Now that I behold the Sage’s countenance, I bathe in and drink from his pure transformation."
Though I am of humble station and remain among the common folk, by encountering the Sage I have entered the ranks of the sublime.
Like the wind brushing through a forest of fragrant trees, my breath merges with it to form a perfumed breeze;
like the various birds gathering on Mount Sumeru, their diverse colors all become one with its golden luster.
Having met with a person of wisdom, one receives their protection and shares in their glory;
as a rustic man, he serves the immortal, becoming a three-legged star in life.
Worldly benefits all come to an end, but the benefits of the Sage are forever inexhaustible.
The king of men has many faults and transgressions; meeting a Sage brings constant peace and benefit.
The Buddha knows that the king’s heart is sincere and that he delights in the Dharma like Śakra;
yet he possesses two kinds of attachment, unable to forget wealth and sensual pleasure.
Knowing the time and knowing the king’s mental disposition, he preached the Dharma for him:
“Even a lowly person of evil karma knows to show respect upon seeing the virtuous;
how much more so for a sovereign king who has accumulated merit and rides upon the power of past causes?”
To encounter a Buddha and show him increased reverence is not what is difficult;
that a kingdom is naturally tranquil and its people at peace is not something increased by seeing a Buddha.
Now I shall briefly explain the Dharma; Great King, listen attentively for a moment.
Uphold what I have taught, and you shall see the fruits of my merit realized.
When life ends and body and spirit part, and all kinsmen are left behind,
only one's good and evil karma follows from beginning to end like a shadow.
One should honor the kingly enterprise of the Dharma and nourish the myriad people as one's own children;
then one’s fame will spread in the present life, and at the end of life, one will ascend to heaven.
If one indulges the passions and does not follow the Dharma, there will be suffering now and no joy hereafter.
In ancient times, King Karṇa, by following the Dharma, received celestial blessings;
King Kalmāṣapāda, having committed evil deeds, was reborn in an evil realm upon the end of his life.
Now, as your great king, I shall briefly explain the teachings of good and evil.
The essential point is to maintain a heart of loving-kindness, viewing all people as if they were one's own only child.
Without oppression or harm, skillfully restrain the sense faculties;
abandon the deviant path to follow the straight road, and do not exalt yourself while disparaging others.
Form friendships with those who practice austerities; do not associate with friends of wrong views.
Do not rely on royal power or authority, and do not listen to the words of the wicked and sycophantic.
Do not cause distress to those practicing austerities, and do not transgress the king’s righteous laws.
Reciting the Buddha's name upholds the True Dharma, subduing those who act contrary to it.
Appearing as the supreme among men, his virtue flourishes within the Way.
Reflect deeply on the perception of impermanence; body and life shift and pass away with every thought-moment.
Settling the mind in lofty and sublime realms, one aspires to reach the ford of cool serenity;
preserving the bliss of compassionate sovereignty, one increases joy in future lives,
and by transmitting one's fame through vast eons, one surely repays the grace of the Tathāgata.
Just as one who loves sweet fruit must plant its fine seeds,
so too there are those who enter from light into darkness, those who enter from darkness into light,
those for whom darkness follows upon darkness, and those for whom light is the cause of further light.
The wise abandon the three grades [of unwholesome action] and should study clarity from beginning to end.
When evil words are spoken, the crowd responds; when good is proclaimed, followers are rare.
There is no action that does not bear fruit; that which is done shall never perish.
If one does not diligently practice at the outset of establishing oneself, one will ultimately be unable to achieve anything.
If one has not cultivated the causes of goodness from the start, there will be no such joy later on.
Since the past offers no period of rest, one ought therefore to cultivate goodness.
Reflecting inwardly that one does no evil, yet because one creates for oneself, one must receive the retribution;
it is like the convergence of four stone mountains, leaving sentient beings with no place to flee.
Amidst the mountains of birth, old age, sickness, and death, there is no way for the multitude of living beings to escape.
Only by practicing the True Dharma can one emerge from this mountain of heavy suffering.
The world is entirely impermanent; the realm of the five desires is like a flash of lightning.
At the very tip of the point of old age and death, how could one practice what is not the Dharma?
The victorious kings of antiquity were like the Lord of Gods (Īśvara);
though their valorous wills soared through the void, they vanished as soon as they appeared.
The kalpa-fire melts Mount Sumeru, and the waters of the ocean are utterly dried up.
How much more so this body, which is like foam or a bubble— how could it be expected to endure long in the world?
When fierce winds cease at Mount Sumeru, when the sun’s light is eclipsed by Mount Meru,
and when a blazing fire is extinguished by water— all things inevitably return to extinction.
This body is an impermanent vessel, guarded with great effort through the long night;
extensively provided for with wealth and beauty, it gives rise to negligence and arrogance.
When the time of death suddenly arrives, it becomes as rigid as a withered tree.
When a person of wisdom perceives this transformation, how could they practice diligently while remaining in sleep?
Birth and death alone set the mechanism in motion; if one does not stop, one will surely fall.
Do not cultivate nor continue in pleasure; those who receive bitter retribution do not engage in such things.
Do not associate with inferior friends; do not study that which does not sever ignorance.
Study that which leads to the wisdom of non-attachment to existence; through such acceptance, one shall surely become bodiless.
To possess a body while remaining unstained by objects is rare; to be stained by objects is a great fault.
Though one may be born among the gods of the formless realm, one cannot escape the passage of time and change.
One should train in the unchanging body; being unchanging, there is no fault.
Because this body exists, it is the root of all suffering.
Therefore, all wise ones bring their fundamental nature to rest in the bodiless.
All classes of sentient beings arise from desire;
thus, regarding the existence of desire, one should give rise to a mind of weary detachment.
One who is weary of and detached from sensual existence will not undergo manifold sufferings.
Even birth in the realms of form or formlessness involves the great affliction of change, for they lack true tranquility;
how much more so for those who have not abandoned sensual desire?
Thus one contemplates the three realms: impermanent and without a master, with manifold sufferings constantly ablaze—how could a wise person take delight in them?
Like a tree engulfed in a raging fire, how could flocks of birds gather there?
The awakened one is a man of light; apart from this, there is no light.
This is the opening of awakening; apart from this, there is no awakening.
This is what should be done; apart from this, it is not to be done.
This constitutes the proximate tenet; to depart from this is to contradict the principle.
To say that this sublime Dharma is not for those in the household life is a false teaching;
the Dharma is propagated solely by means of persons.
When those afflicted by heat enter cold water, they all attain refreshing coolness;
when a lamp’s light shines in a dark room, everyone beholds the five colors.
The cultivation of the Way is likewise: there is no difference between the monastic and the lay.
Some fall into transgression while dwelling in the mountains; others ascend to the rank of immortals while remaining at home.
Ignorance is a vast ocean, and false views are its surging waves;
sentient beings follow the current of craving, drifting and turning about, unable to cross over.
Wisdom is a light boat, held steady by the correctness of samādhi;
with skillful means as the oars and mindfulness as the rudder, one can cross the ocean of ignorance.
At that time, the king listened with single-minded devotion to what the Omniscient One had spoken.
He grew weary of worldly glory and realized that even for a king there is no true joy;
like an elephant in rut that has escaped its bonds, he returned once his intoxication had fully subsided.
At that time, various non-Buddhists, seeing that the king placed his faith and reverence in the Buddha, [were filled with resentment].
They all entreated the Great King, "Grant us a contest of supernatural powers with the Buddha.
Then the King addressed the World-Honored One, "I pray that you grant their request.
The Buddha immediately granted his silent assent.
The immortals possessing the five supernatural powers all came to where the Buddha was;
the Buddha immediately manifested his spiritual power, sitting upright upon a pedestal in mid-air.
He radiated great light everywhere, like the brilliance of the morning sun.
Having completely subdued all non-Buddhists, the people of the kingdom universally turned to him as their refuge.
For the sake of preaching the Dharma to his mother, he ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
for three months he dwelt in the celestial palace, universally transforming all devas and humans.
Having completed her repayment of gratitude to Tārā, she returned at the conclusion of the summer retreat;
accompanied by a host of devas, she descended upon a staircase of the seven jewels to Jambudvīpa,
the place where all Buddhas constantly descend.
Immeasurable devas and humans, riding in celestial palaces, escorted her along;
the lords and subjects of Jambudvīpa joined their palms and gazed upward.
The Mother who teaches in the heavens, together with the other hosts of devas—
Returning to wander among humans, he traveled and transformed beings according to conditions:
Jyotiṣka and Jīvaka, Śūra and Śroṇa,
the elder’s son Aṅga, and Prince Abhaya.
Nigrodha and others, Śrīguptaka,
and Nirgrantha Upāli— he caused them all to attain liberation.
The King of Gandhāra, whose name was Puṣkarasārin, [was also liberated].
Having heard the teaching of the subtle and wondrous Dharma, he abandoned his kingdom and went forth into homelessness.
On Mount Vipula, he subdued and converted the yakṣas Haimavata and Pāṭakīla.
In the Pārāyana, among the brahmins on Mount Paṃsukūla,
he subdued them through the subtle meaning of a half-verse and inspired them with faith and joy.
In the village of Thaṇamati, there was Koṭa Taṇḍi.
These two are the leaders of those who extensively slaughter living beings for sacrificial rites;
through the Tathāgata’s skillful means of transformation, he causes them to enter the Right Path.
On Mount Videha, there is a deity of great majesty and power.
In Pañcaśikhā, he received the certainty of entering the Dharma;
in the village of Viṇhuṣṭha, he transformed the mother of Nanda;
in the city of Aṅgāpuri, he subdued the powerful deity.
Punabhadda and Sulludantaka were fierce and powerful dragons;
the king and his entire harem all received the True Dharma.
In that village of dwarfs, Keṇa and Śila,
who sought the pleasures of rebirth in heaven, were transformed and led into the True Path.
Aṅgulimāla, in that village of Sūmāra—
To manifest supernatural powers and transform them so they were immediately subdued.
There was a son of a great elder, Pūlijiava by name;
he was immensely wealthy with vast riches, like Punabhadra.
Thereupon, in the presence of the Tathāgata, he received transformation and practiced giving extensively.
In that village of Bhaddiya, he transformed Bhaddiya-putta and the two brothers, the spirits Bhadra and Bhadra-putta.
In Videha and Pūrvavideha, there were two brahmins:
one named Mahāyus and the other named Brahmāyus;
through debate he subdued them and caused them to enter the True Dharma.
Arriving at the city of Vaiśālī, he converted the various rākṣasa demons,
as well as the Licchavis and Siṃha, along with the entire multitude of Licchavis and Saccaka the Nirgrantha;
he caused them all to enter the True Dharma.
At Āmalakapāda, there was the yakṣa Bhadra, as well as Bhadraka and Bhadrajāma;
then he went to Mount Ālaka and delivered the yakṣa Ālamba.
The second was named Kumāra, and the third was Haṃsika.
Returning to Mount Gaja, he delivered the ghost Gaṅgana,
as well as the yakṣa Sūcīlomā and his sister’s son.
Again he went to Vārāṇasī and converted Kātyāyana.
Thereafter, riding upon his supernatural powers,
he went to Śūrpāraka and converted those merchants, as well as Trapuṣa and Bhallika.
He accepted the sandalwood hall, whose exquisite fragrance flows on to this day.
Reaching Mahābodhi, he delivered the sage Kapila;
there the Muni dwelt, treading upon the stone with his feet.
The thousand-spoked double wheels appeared, never to be worn away.
Reaching the place of Pāraṇa, he transformed the ghost Pāraṇa.
Arriving at the kingdom of Mathurā, he delivered the ghost Ghaṭotkaca.
At Thullakoṭṭhita, he ordained Dārucīriya.
At the village of Veḷudvāra, he ordained many brahmins.
At the village of Kallavāḷamuttagāma, he ordained Sappadasa.
He likewise transformed them there— Agni and Viśākha.
Returning again to the kingdom of Śrāvastī,
he delivered Gautama, Jātiyu, Luṇa, and Dakācālī.
Returning to the kingdom of Kośala, he converted the teacher of the non-Buddhists,
Pukkusāti, as well as the assembly of brahmins.
Arriving at Setavyā, he stayed in a place of tranquil seclusion.
He delivered various non-Buddhist seers, causing them to enter the path of the Buddha-seers.
Arriving at the kingdom of Aśvaja, he delivered the hosts of ghosts and nāgas.
Reaching the kingdom of Śabira, he delivered two evil dragon kings.
One was named Kumbhīra, and the second was named Karaka. Again,
arriving at the kingdom of Vatsa, he transformed and delivered the yakṣas and spirits,
whose names were Vaiśravaṇa and Nāgula, along with their parents.
And also the great elder, causing them to believe and delight in the True Dharma;
arriving at the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, he transformed and delivered Ghoṣila,
as well as the two female lay disciples, Vatsa and Uttarā.
The female lay disciples and their companions were saved in successive order;
reaching the kingdom of Gandhāra, she saved the dragon Apalāla.
Following such a sequence, she delivered those of aerial, aquatic, and terrestrial natures.
He went everywhere to transform and deliver beings, like the sun illuminating the dark and hidden.
At that time, Devadatta, seeing the Buddha’s extraordinary virtues,
harbored jealousy in his heart and fell away from all his meditative concentrations.
Having devised various evil means to destroy the True Dharma and the Saṃgha,
he climbed Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and hurled down a boulder to strike the Buddha;
the stone split into two parts and fell to the Buddha’s left and right.
Upon the King’s level and straight path, he released a wild and intoxicated evil elephant;
its thunderous roar was like crashing peals of lightning,
its courageous spirit surged into clouds as it charged headlong and ran amok, leaping over obstacles like a violent wind.
With a nose, tusks, and a tail, and four legs, wherever it touches, nothing remains uncrushed.
In the streets and alleys of Rājagṛha, people lie slaughtered in disarray;
corpses are strewn across the roads, with marrow and brains and blood flowing everywhere.
All the men and women were so terrified they did not venture out their doors;
the entire city was filled with trembling, hearing only the sounds of panicked cries.
Some fled from the city in haste, while others hid themselves within caves and burrows.
The Tathāgata’s assembly of five hundred followed him as he reached the time to enter the city;
people at the windows of the high pavilions entreated the Buddha not to proceed.
The Tathāgata’s mind was peaceful and composed; with a serene countenance, he remained free from fear.
Meditating only on the suffering of greed and envy, he wished with a compassionate heart to bring peace.
Surrounded by a host of devas and nāgas, he gradually approached the place where the mad elephant was;
while the other bhikṣus fled, he remained there together only with Ānanda.
Just as the various characteristics of phenomena, though diverse, do not shift from their single intrinsic nature,
so too the intoxicated elephant, roused by wild fury, had his mind instantly awakened upon seeing the Buddha.
He cast himself down to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, like the collapsing of Mount Tai.
The Lotus-Palm Hand rubbed his head, like the sun shining upon dark clouds.
Prostrating himself at the Buddha’s feet, [the Buddha] spoke these words of Dharma:
“O Elephant, do not harm the Great Dragon; it is difficult for an elephant to fight a dragon.”
An elephant wishing to harm a great dragon will never be reborn in a happy realm.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are intoxicated and difficult to subdue, yet the Buddha has already subdued them.
Therefore, on this day, you should abandon greed, hatred, and delusion.
Already submerged in the mire of suffering, he did not abandon it and sank even deeper.
When that elephant heard the Buddha’s teaching, his intoxication was dispelled and his mind immediately attained awakening;
his body and mind found peace and happiness, like one who drinks nectar when thirsty.
The elephant has already been transformed by the Buddha; the people of the land are all filled with joy.
They all exclaim in praise of this rarity and present various kinds of offerings.
Those of inferior goodness turn into middling, and those of middling goodness advance to the superior.
Those without faith conceived it, and those already faithful became deeply rooted in it.
When King Ajātaśatru saw the Buddha subdue the intoxicated elephant, a sense of wonder arose in his heart;
his joy redoubled and his reverence increased.
The Tathāgata, through skillful means, manifests various supernatural powers to subdue all sentient beings;
according to their capacities, they enter the True Dharma,
and the entire nation cultivates wholesome deeds, just like the people at the beginning of the kalpa.
That Devadatta, bound by his own evil deeds,
who formerly possessed the supernatural power of flight, now falls into the Avīci Hell.
When the World-Honored One had finished his extensive work of conversion, Devadatta conceived the thought of nirvāṇa.
Setting out from Rājagṛha, he proceeded to Pāṭaliputra.
Having arrived, he stayed there at the Bārhadratha-caitya;
that was a border town and a tributary state of Magadha.
The Brahmin who was lord of the land, Learned and clear in the scriptures,
Who observed the signs of the realm’s safety and peril, Was the teacher upon whom the nation relied.
The King of Magadha dispatched a messenger To issue an edict to that observer.
The mandate arises from the fortified city, established to guard against powerful neighbors.
The World-Honored One has prophesied that land, which the celestial deities shall protect;
therein one shall build cities and walls, forever secure and never falling into ruin.
Gazing upward with hearts full of joy, they together made offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
As the Buddha emerged from that city gate, he proceeded to the banks of the Ganges.
Gazing up with profound reverence for the Buddha, it was called the Gate of Gautama.
The people along the banks of the Ganges all came out to welcome the World-Honored One,
offering various kinds of provisions and each preparing their boats for him to cross.
Because there were so many boats, the World-Honored One, fearing it would be partial and contrary to the hearts of the multitude, [did not accept them].
By means of supernormal powers, he and his great assembly concealed their bodies;
suddenly vanishing from this shore, they emerged upon the other shore.
Having boarded the vessel of wisdom, he extensively delivers all sentient beings.
By the power of this merit, they crossed the river without relying on a boat.
The people along the banks of the Ganges raised their voices in unison, crying out in wonder:
"How marvelous! Let us all call this ford by the name of Gautama’s Ford."
The city gate was named Gautama Gate, and the ferry was named Gautama Ferry;
these names have circulated through the world, handed down and praised by successive generations.
The Tathāgata proceeded further and arrived at that village of Kūṭi.
Having taught the Dharma and transformed many beings, he again arrived at the village of Nadika.
Many of the people there had died of pestilence, and their relatives all came to inquire:
"Regarding those kinsmen who have died of pestilence, where are they reborn after the end of their lives?"
The Buddha, who thoroughly understands the retribution of karma, answers every question as it is asked.
Having previously arrived at Vaiśālī, he dwelt in the Āmra Grove.
There, the lady Āmrapālī, hearing that the Buddha had come to her park, [welcomed him].
A multitude of handmaidens followed in attendance, emerging with measured grace to welcome him.
Skillfully restraining all the sensory faculties, she wore light, plain garments;
having cast off her ornate finery, she bathed herself with fragrant flowers.
Like a virtuous woman of the world, pure and simple as she worships Heaven,
with a dignified and wondrous countenance, her form like that of a celestial jade maiden.
The Buddha, seeing the woman approaching from afar, addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"This woman is exceedingly beautiful, capable of captivating the hearts of practitioners.
You all should maintain right mindfulness and subdue your minds with wisdom.
It would be better to be in the mouth of a fierce tiger or beneath the sharp blade of a madman," than to fall under her influence.
One should not give rise to feelings of lustful desire toward women.
Whether they manifest seductive gestures while walking, standing, sitting, or reclining,
or even in the form of painted images, they all display their coquettish countenances.
They plunder the virtuous mind of others; how can one not guard against them?

The mind is constantly filled with fear, and ill repute follows like a shadow;

Therefore, the wise person should cultivate pure ethical discipline.

the pure precepts act as a staircase, enabling people to ascend to heaven.

First, one should abandon the notion of "mine," for the sense of "mine" obscures all virtues.

Arrogance and indolence extinguish shame and remorse, while sorrow and grief weaken even the strongest will.

the loss of all meritorious qualities is entirely due to harboring pride.
I am superior among the superior, my virtues are equal to those of the most excellent;
yet if I were slightly inferior to the superior, I would be a fool indeed.
Physical form and lineage are entirely impermanent, flickering and never remaining still for a moment.
All things are subject to decay; what use is pride?
Greed is a great affliction; feigning intimacy while harboring secret enmity, a fierce fire breaks out from within—so too does the fire of greed.
The blazing of greed is more intense than the fires of the world;
while a raging fire can be extinguished by water, craving is difficult to eliminate.
When a fierce fire consumes the wilderness, the grass is exhausted only to grow back again.
When the fire of craving burns the mind, it is difficult for the True Dharma to arise.
Craving seeks worldly pleasure, and as that pleasure increases, impure karma grows;
through evil karma one falls into the miserable realms—there is no enemy greater than craving.
Greed gives rise to craving; craving leads to the habitual pursuit of desires.
This pursuit of desire invites manifold sufferings; no evil is more fundamental than greed.
Greed is a great malady that the wise remedy with the medicine of wisdom, while the foolish merely cease [from it] through ignorance.
Erroneous perceptions and improper reflection can cause craving to increase. Through the wisdom of true contemplation—
that all things are impermanent, suffering, impure, and devoid of self or what belongs to a self—
one can extinguish that false craving.
Therefore, regarding sense objects, one should cultivate the contemplation of reality;
once the contemplation of reality has arisen, one attains liberation from craving.
Seeing virtues gives rise to craving; seeing faults gives rise to aversion.
When virtue surpasses both, they are forgotten; greed and anger are thereby extinguished.
Anger alters one’s natural countenance and can destroy a beautiful appearance;
anger clouds the clear eyes and harms the Dharma and its meaning that one wishes to hear.
One who severs the bonds of affection is held in contempt by the world.
Therefore, one should abandon anger and not follow a hateful mind;
he who can restrain the wild and angry heart is called a skilled driver.

If a person gives rise to hatred and resentment, they first burn their own heart.
Then one inflicts [suffering] upon others, whether by burning them or not;
the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death oppress sentient beings,
yet one further adds anger and harm, multiplying enmity where there is already much enmity.
Seeing the world oppressed by manifold sufferings, one should give rise to a heart of compassion;
as sentient beings give rise to afflictions, they increase in measureless variations from subtle to gross.
Through the Tathāgata’s skillful means, he provides brief explanations according to their specific ailments.

Venerable Ānanda, seeing the earth tremble everywhere, [He realized the Master had passed away.]

the principle of affection is not eternal, so you should abandon the heart of sorrowful attachment.

One remains far removed from the perception of pleasure;
the arising, abiding, and ceasing of mind and consciousness do not pause for even a moment, renewing themselves incessantly.

Through contemplation and correct observation, this is the path of the One Vehicle.

all living beings are deeply to be pitied, like people who have lost their divine power—the whole world mourns them together.

With right contemplation abiding in the mind, one remains ever awake even while sleeping.
