weeping as he went, he followed the teaching, completed the arrangements, and returned to report.
The Tathāgata approached the rope-couch and lay down on his right side with his head toward the north.
Resting his hand upon his crossed legs, like a lion king,
having brought an end to suffering in this final body, he lies down once and shall never rise again.
Surrounded by a multitude of disciples, they lament that the Eye of the World has been extinguished.
The winds have ceased and the forest streams are still; birds and beasts are silent and without sound.
The sap flows like tears from the trees, and flowers and leaves fall out of season;
gods and humans who have not yet abandoned desire are all utterly terrified.
Like a person wandering through a vast marsh, on a perilous path before reaching a village,
fearing they may not arrive and with a heart full of dread, their form is hurried and anxious.
Thus the Tathāgata, lying down for the final time, addressed Ānanda:
"Go and inform the Mallas: 'The time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived.
If they do not see me, they will forever harbor regret and give rise to great suffering.
Ānanda received the Buddha’s instruction and followed the road, weeping with grief.
He addressed those Mallas:
"The World-Honored One has reached his ultimate end.
When the Mallas heard this, they were struck with extreme and great terror.
Men and women rushed out, wailing and weeping as they reached the Buddha’s dwelling;
clad in tattered garments with disheveled hair, covered in dust and with sweat streaming down their bodies,
they went to that grove in utter lamentation, like those whose heavenly merit has been exhausted.
With tears streaming down, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; their bodies withered and frail from grief and sorrow.
The Tathāgata comforted them, saying:
“Do not be distressed or dejected. Now is the time for sympathetic joy; it is not fitting to give way to sorrow and lamentation.”
That which was the aim throughout long kalpas, I have now finally attained:
the realm beyond the senses, the inexhaustible and cool state.
Free from earth, water, fire, and wind, it is tranquil, without arising or ceasing.
Having forever eliminated all sorrow and affliction, why do you grieve for me?
In the past, on Mount Gaja, I sought to cast off this body;
yet, due to the power of past causes and conditions, I remain in the world until this day.
Guarding this fragile body as if dwelling with a venomous serpent, I now enter great tranquility;
the conditions for all suffering have come to an end.
No longer shall I receive another body, and future suffering is forever stilled.
"You should no longer cause me such terror.
When the Mallas heard the Buddha's words, they entered into great tranquility;
their minds were agitated and their vision grew dim, as if beholding a vast, profound darkness.
Joining their palms, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Buddha has departed from the suffering of birth and death for the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa; We truly rejoice in this!
It is like one who, from a burning house, Is personally rescued from a raging fire.”
Even the devas are filled with joy; how much more so the people of the world?
Since the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, sentient beings have nothing left to behold.
They are forever separated from their protector; for this reason, they give rise to sorrow and grief.
For example, like a multitude of merchants traveling far across a vast wilderness,
who have but a single guide that suddenly perishes midway;
the great assembly has no one to rely upon— how could they not be filled with grief and sorrow?
Having personally realized it in this very life and beholding all with knowledge and vision,
yet failing to attain the supreme victory, one will be ridiculed by the whole world;
like a fool guarding a mountain of jewels while remaining in poverty and suffering.
Thus did these Mallas lament before the Buddha,
like a single child lamenting before a compassionate father.
With words of skillful guidance, the Buddha revealed the ultimate truth.
He addressed the assembly of Mallas:
"It is truly as you have said; one must be diligent in seeking the Way;
it is not through merely seeing me that one attains it."
If one practices according to what I have taught, one will escape the net of all suffering.
To practice the Way, it must reside in the mind; it does not necessarily depend on seeing me.
It is like a sick person who relies on a prescription to take effective medicine.
All ailments will naturally be eliminated without waiting to see a physician.
It is not as good as practicing according to my teaching; seeing me in vain is of no benefit.
Though one may be far from me in body, practicing the Dharma brings one close to me.
If one dwells together with others but does not follow the Dharma, know that such a person is far from me.
Restrain the mind and do not be negligent; apply yourself with diligence to cultivating right action.
When human beings are born into this world, they are oppressed by manifold sufferings throughout the long night.
Agitated and unable to find peace, like a lamp in the wind; at that time,
the multitude of Mallas, hearing the Buddha’s compassionate instruction,
were moved within and their tears fell, yet they forcibly restrained themselves and returned home.
At that time there was a brahmin named Subhadra,
who was fully endowed with noble virtue and protected sentient beings through pure precepts.
Having been influenced by false views since youth, he had practiced as an ascetic in a non-Buddhist sect.
Desiring to come and see the World-Honored One, he addressed Ānanda:
"I have heard of the Way of the Tathāgata; its meaning is profound and difficult to fathom.
He is the Unsurpassed Awakened One in the world, the foremost Teacher who tames others."
Now he desires to enter parinirvāṇa; he will be difficult to encounter again.
One who is difficult to see has been seen, yet such a sight is as rare as the moon reflected in a mirror.
I now desire to behold him, the unsurpassed and virtuous Guide.
Seeking to escape all suffering and cross to the other shore of birth and death, the Buddha-sun is about to withdraw its light; I pray that I may behold it for a brief moment.
Ānanda’s heart was moved by grief, and he further thought it a mere mockery.
Some rejoice at the World-Honored One’s passing, thinking it improper for the Buddha to see them;
knowing their aspirations and that they were fit vessels for the True Dharma,
he addressed Ānanda:
“Listen, before those non-Buddhists arrive, I have come to deliver living beings; do not create obstacles.
Upon hearing this, Subhadra felt great joy in his heart;
his affection for the Dharma deepened further, and he approached the Buddha with increased reverence.
Speaking words that were timely and appropriate, he greeted him with gentle speech and,
with a serene countenance and palms joined, requested:
"I now wish to ask a question."
In this world, there are many like me who know the Dharma;
yet I have heard only of the unique and essential path to liberation attained by the Buddha.
I pray that you will briefly explain it for me, so as to quench my parched heart with its refreshing moisture.
Not for the sake of debate, nor with a mind intent on victory or defeat,
the Buddha briefly expounded the Eightfold Noble Path for that brahmin.
Upon hearing it, he immediately received it with an open heart, like one who has lost his way finding the correct path.
Realizing that what was previously studied was not the ultimate path,
he immediately attained what he had never heard before and abandoned the wrong ways.
Turning his back on the obstacles of delusion and darkness, he reflected upon what he had formerly practiced.
When hatred and the darkness of delusion coexist, they nurture unwholesome karma.
While the practice of desire, hatred, and delusion can give rise to various wholesome karmas,
even the wisdom of extensive learning and diligence arise from the presence of desire.
If hatred and delusion are severed, one is then free from all karmas;
once all karmas have been eliminated, this is called liberation from karma.
One who is liberated from karma does not correspond with [the notion of] an object.
The world says that all things possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If there were such an intrinsic nature in craving, hatred, and delusion, they would have to exist eternally; how then could there be liberation?
Even if hatred and delusion are extinguished, craving arises once again; just as the nature of water is cold, yet it becomes hot through the condition of fire,
so too, when the heat subsides, it returns to its natural state of cold, for its intrinsic nature is constant.
One should know that when the nature of craving exists, the wisdom gained through hearing and diligence do not increase;
since they neither increase nor decrease, how can this be liberation?
It was previously said that birth and death originally arise from within this very nature.
Now, observing that principle, there is no one who attains liberation.
If nature were eternally abiding, how could there be a final consummation?
It is like lighting a bright lamp; how could one ever cause it to be without light?
The true meaning of the Buddha-way is this: the world arises conditioned by craving;
when craving ceases, there is tranquility, for with the cessation of the cause, the fruit perishes.
Originally, one thought the self was distinct from the body, yet one does not perceive a non-agent.
Now that I have heard the Buddha’s true teaching, I know there is no self in the world.
All phenomena arise from causes and conditions; because they lack independence, they are born of causes and conditions and are thus suffering;
their cessation through causes and conditions is likewise so.
Observing that things arise through causes and conditions, one then eliminates the view of nihilism;
seeing that the world ceases when conditions disperse, one then leaves behind the view of eternalism.
Completely relinquishing all prior views, one deeply perceives the Buddha’s True Dharma.
Having planted seeds of goodness in past lives, one is able to awaken immediately upon hearing the Dharma;
having already attained sublime tranquility, one reaches the cool and inexhaustible state.
With the mind opened and faith expanded, one gazes up at the Tathāgata lying in repose.
Unable to bear the sight of the Tathāgata entering parinirvāṇa in this world while the Buddha’s ultimate purpose remains unfulfilled, I shall first attain extinction.
Joining my palms in reverence before the holy countenance, I sit upright upon my seat.
Having relinquished his life, he entered parinirvāṇa, like rain extinguishing a small fire.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"My final disciple has now entered parinirvāṇa; you all should make offerings to him."
When the first watch of the night had passed, the moon was bright and the stars were clear;
in the secluded grove, all was silent and still. Then the Buddha gave rise to a heart of great compassion and left these final instructions to his disciples:
You all should revere the Prātimokṣa;
it is your great teacher, a bright lamp in the long night,
and a great treasure for the poor.
Regarding those whom you are instructed and admonished, you should follow them in accordance with my teachings,
no differently than how you serve me. You should purify the conduct of body and speech, and abandon all occupations for livelihood,
such as fields, houses, and raising livestock, as well as the accumulation of wealth and the five grains.
One should avoid all these things, as one would shun a great pit of fire:
tilling the soil and cutting down trees and grasses, practicing medicine to treat various ailments,
gazing upward at the calculations of the calendar, and calculating the signs of good and ill fortune through the movements of the stars.
One should not engage in divination regarding profit or loss;

one should restrain the body and eat according to the season. One should not accept commissions to practice arts, nor mix medicinal decoctions, and should remain far removed from all forms of flattery and crookedness.
One should know the proper measure when receiving requisites for life in accordance with the Dharma;
receiving them without hoarding—this is a brief explanation of the precepts.
They are the root of all precepts and also the foundation of liberation.
Relying on this Dharma, one can give rise to all meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and all true wisdom (*jñāna*).
By taking this as the object of focus, one attains the ultimate;
therefore, you should uphold it and not allow it to be severed or destroyed.
Because pure precepts are uninterrupted, there are all wholesome dharmas;
without them, there are no wholesome dharmas, for it is by means of the precepts that they are established.
Having already abided in pure precepts, one skillfully restrains all the sensory faculties.
Just as a skilled cowherd does not allow his cattle to run wild,

one who fails to restrain the horses of the sense-faculties and lets them roam unrestrained among the six objects will bring about calamity in this present life and is destined to fall into the evil realms.
Just as an unbroken horse causes its rider to fall into a pit, so the wise person should not let their sense faculties run wild.
These faculties are extremely fierce and evil; they are man’s greatest enemy.
Sentient beings cherish their sense faculties, yet they are harmed by those very same things.
Deep-seated enmity, virulent venomous snakes, fierce tigers, and raging fires—
these are the greatest evils in the world, yet the wise do not fear them.
I fear only the light and fickle mind, which leads people into evil realms;
for it delights in petty tranquility and fails to perceive the deep precipices.
Like a mad elephant that has lost its goad, or a monkey that has found a forest.
The restless mind is thus; the wise should restrain it.
If one lets the mind run wild and act as it pleases, one will never attain nirvana.
Therefore, one should subdue the mind and hasten toward a place of tranquility.
Know moderation in eating and drinking, as one would when taking medicine;
do not give rise to greed or anger on account of food.
Food and drink merely serve to stave off hunger and thirst, like oil applied to a dilapidated cart.
Just as a bee gathers from a flower, Without destroying its color or fragrance,
So should a bhikṣu go for alms, Not injuring the donor’s faith.
If a person opens their heart to give, One should consider what they can afford.
Do not underestimate the strength of an ox, lest you overload it and cause it injury.
During the three periods of morning, noon, and evening, cultivate right action in succession;
likewise, during the first and last watches of the night, do not indulge in sleep.
At midnight, settle the mind and lie down, fixing the attention upon the sign of light.
Do not sleep through the entire night, causing body and life to pass in vain;
since the fire of time constantly burns the body, how can one sleep so long?
The various enemies that are the afflictions Ride upon emptiness and follow to harm;
When the mind is clouded by sleep, Who can awaken when death arrives?
A venomous snake hidden in one’s house Can be driven out by a skillful spell.
The black viper dwells within the heart; clear awakening is the skillful incantation that removes it.
To remain in long sleep without such a rite is the mark of a person devoid of shame.
Shame and modesty are one’s ornamental robes; shame is the hook that restrains the elephant.
A sense of shame and dread of blame bring the mind to stability; lack of shame destroys the roots of goodness.
Those with shame and dread of blame are praised as noble by the world; those without shame belong to the ranks of birds and beasts.
Even if someone were to take a sharp blade and dismember one's body limb by limb, [one with shame would endure it].
One should not harbor resentment or anger, nor utter harsh words with an evil mind;
such speech harms oneself but does not harm others.
To discipline the body and practice asceticism is not superior to the excellence of patience.
Only by practicing patience does one possess a firm strength that is difficult to overcome;
therefore, harbor no resentment and do not address others with harsh words.
Anger destroys the True Dharma and likewise ruins a beautiful countenance.
One loses a good reputation, and the fire of anger burns one's own heart;
anger is the enemy of merit—cherish virtue and harbor no resentment.
Since there are many afflictions in the household life, it is not surprising that one feels anger.
To leave the household life while harboring anger is to contradict the Dharma;
it is like having a blazing fire within cold water.
If a mind of pride arises, one should touch one's own head with one's own hand.
Having shaved your hair and donned dyed robes, holding an alms-bowl in hand,
you live by begging for sustenance at the outskirts— why then do you give rise to pride?
Even the pride of worldly people regarding the color of their clothes or their lineage is a fault.
How much more so for those who have left the household life, whose resolve is to seek the path of liberation—
how could they give rise to a mind of arrogance?
This would be utterly unacceptable.
Crookedness and rectitude are contrary in nature; they cannot coexist, just as frost and fire.
One who has left the household life to cultivate the straight path should not employ flattery or crookedness.
Deceit, hypocrisy, illusion, and falsehood are improper; only the Dharma is free from deception and fraud.
Much seeking leads to suffering; few desires lead to peace and security.
To attain peace, one should have few desires—how much more so when seeking true liberation?
Out of stinginess, people fear seeking much, for they dread the depletion of their wealth and treasures.
Even those who are fond of giving fear that their wealth may not suffice;
therefore, one should have few desires and bestow upon others a mind free from fear.
Through this mind of few desires, one attains the path of liberation.
If you wish to seek liberation, you should likewise practice contentment.
One who is content is always joyful; joy itself is the Dharma.
Though one's means of livelihood may be humble, through contentment one is ever at peace.
The person who lacks contentment, though they may attain the bliss of rebirth in heaven,
because of their lack of contentment, the fire of suffering constantly burns their heart.
To be wealthy yet lacking contentment is itself the suffering of poverty.
Though poor, one who knows contentment is the most wealthy of all.
As for those who lack contentment, the objects of the five desires become ever more vast;
yet they seek further without satiety, suffering as they gallop through the long night.
Constantly striving with anxious concern, one instead brings sorrow to those who know contentment;
by not gathering many followers, one’s mind remains ever peaceful and secure.
Because of this peace and tranquility, humans and devas alike offer their service.
Therefore, one should abandon both close and distant kinsmen.
Like a solitary tree in a vast marsh where many birds gather to roost, so it is with those who keep many followers;
through the long night they undergo manifold sufferings.
With many people and many fetters, like an old elephant mired in mud,
if a person exerts diligent effort, there is no benefit they shall not obtain;
therefore, day and night, one should be diligent and never indolent.
A slight stream in the mountains and valleys, by flowing constantly, cuts through rock;
If one drills for fire without diligence, one will toil in vain and gain nothing.
Therefore, one should be diligent, like a strong man drilling for fire.
Though a virtuous friend be excellent, he does not equal right mindfulness;
when right mindfulness dwells in the mind, no evils can enter.
Therefore, the practitioner should always maintain mindfulness of the body.
If one loses mindfulness regarding the body, all wholesome qualities will be forgotten.
Just as a valiant general, clad in armor, confronts a powerful enemy,
so too does right mindfulness serve as heavy armor, capable of subduing the thieves of the six sense objects.
With right concentration, one examines the mind and observes the arising and ceasing of the world;
therefore, the practitioner should practice *samādhi*.
Once tranquility is attained through *samādhi*, one can extinguish all suffering.
Wisdom can illuminate and bring one far from grasping;
contemplating with equanimity and reflecting within, one follows and proceeds toward the True Dharma.
Whether living as a householder or having gone forth, this is the path by which one should travel.
In the great ocean of birth, old age, and death, wisdom is the light boat;
In the vast darkness of ignorance, wisdom is the bright lamp;
For the afflictions, fetters, stains, and diseases, wisdom is the excellent medicine.
The forest of thorns that are the afflictions has wisdom as its sharp axe;
the swift-flowing torrent of delusion and craving has wisdom as its bridge.
Therefore, one should diligently practice the wisdom born of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
One who has accomplished the three kinds of wisdom, though blind, possesses the penetrating eye of insight;
one whose mind lacks wisdom is hypocritical, and such a person is not a renunciant.
Therefore, one should awaken to this and abandon all hypocritical dharmas.
One attains subtle and wondrous bliss, the place of tranquility and security.
By honoring and following heedfulness, one recognizes that heedlessness is the enemy of virtue.
If a person is not heedless, they shall be born in the realm of Śakra.
Those who indulge their minds in negligence will fall among the asuras.
My work of consolation and compassion is now complete;
you all should apply yourselves with diligence and cultivate your own practice well.
In the empty and secluded places of mountains and forests, one increases the mind of tranquility.
One should diligently exhort oneself, lest there be regret later.
Just as a skilled physician of the world prescribes remedies according to the illness, so should one act.
To fail to take medicine while suffering from illness is not the fault of the skilled physician.
I have already spoken the truth and revealed the path of equanimity;
that one hears it yet does not practice it is not the fault of the speaker.
"Regarding the meaning of the Four Noble Truths, whatever you have not yet understood, you should now ask all of it;
do not conceal what is in your hearts.
Out of compassion, the World-Honored One thus instructed them, and the assembly remained silent.
At that time, Aniruddha, having observed the great assembly, remained silent and free from doubt; joining his palms, he addressed the Buddha:
“The moon is warm and the sun’s light is cold; the wind is still and the nature of the earth is mobile.”
Thus, these four kinds of delusions have entirely vanished from the world.
The truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path have never been contradicted in their reality;
as the World-Honored One has taught them, the entire assembly is now free from doubt.
Only upon the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One did everyone feel profound grief;
they did not conceive the thought that the World-Honored One’s teaching was incomplete.
This was true even for those who had newly gone forth, whose hearts had not yet reached deep understanding.
Having heard these earnest teachings today, all my doubts have been entirely removed.
Having crossed the ocean of birth and death, I am now free from desire and have nothing further to seek;
yet now I feel a deep sense of grief and longing, lamenting how swift is the Buddha’s passing into extinction.
The Buddha, through Āniruddha, spoke of various sorrows and griefs;
then, with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, he comforted him and said:
"Even if one were to remain for an eon, in the end, one must inevitably part."
Though distinct in substance, they are in harmony; by their very nature, they do not abide together eternally.
Having completed the benefit of both self and others, what is the purpose of remaining in emptiness?
Those among devas and humans who were to be delivered have all already attained liberation.
You, my disciples, shall successively uphold the True Dharma;
knowing that all that exists must perish, do not give rise to further grief or sorrow.
You should diligently apply skillful means so as to reach the place where there is no parting.
I have already lit the lamp of wisdom, Shining light to dispel the world’s darkness;
All things in the world are not solid or firm— You all should rejoice in this.
Just as when a kinsman suffers a grave illness, One treats them until they are freed from suffering and affliction.
Having cast off the vessel of suffering and turned against the current of the ocean of birth and death, you are forever free from all afflictions; this too should be rejoiced in.
You should each well protect yourselves and not give rise to negligence.
"All that exists shall return to extinction; I now enter parinirvāṇa.
With these words his speech ceased; this was his final instruction.
He entered the samādhi of the first dhyāna, followed by the nine successive attainments.
In reverse order of meditative attainment, he returned to the first dhyāna;
then, rising from the first dhyāna, he entered the fourth dhyāna.
With a mind free from attachment upon emerging from concentration, he immediately entered nirvana.
Because of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the great earth shook everywhere;
from the sky, fire rained down universally, blazing spontaneously without fuel.
Furthermore, flames rose up from the ground, burning fiercely throughout the eight directions.
Even the palaces of the various devas are likewise ablaze;
thunder shakes heaven and earth, and lightning bolts shatter mountains and rivers,
like the sound of drums struck in battle between the devas and asuras.
Fierce winds rise from all four directions, mountains crumble and rain down dust;
the sun and moon lose their radiance, and clear streams all boil and surge.
The firm forests wither and fade, and flowers and leaves fall out of season.
The Flying Dragon rides upon black clouds; with five heads hanging down, tears flow.
The Four Kings and their retinues harbor grief and present offerings.
The Śuddhāvāsa devas descend from above, standing in attendance within the void of space.
Observing impermanence and change, there is neither sorrow nor joy.
Alas, the world has lost its Teacher; how swiftly his eyes have been extinguished!
The devas of the eight classes fill the entirety of space.
Scattering flowers as an offering, they were sorrowful and their hearts were not glad;
only the Māra King rejoiced, playing music to amuse himself.
Jambudvīpa has lost its glory, like a mountain whose peak has collapsed.
The great elephant’s ivory tusks are broken; the bull-king’s twin horns are shattered.
The void is bereft of sun and moon; the lotus flower meets with bitter frost.
When the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa, the world withers in like manner.
At that time, there was a son of heaven, riding in a palace drawn by a thousand white geese,
who, from the midst of the empty sky above, beheld the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
For the sake of the entire host of devas, he extensively recited these verses on impermanence:
"All phenomena are impermanent; they arise swiftly and perish swiftly.
Their arising is accompanied by suffering; only cessation is bliss.
The fuel of karmic formations has been gathered; the fire of wisdom blazes forth."
The smoke of his fame rises to the heavens, Which the timely rain causes to be extinguished;
Just as when the fire at the end of an eon arises, It is extinguished by the calamity of water.
Furthermore, there is the Brahma-seer deity, Who is like the Seer of the Ultimate Truth.
Dwelling in the supreme and wondrous bliss of the heavens, yet unstained by celestial retribution,
he praised the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, his mind composed as he spoke these words:
“Observing the phenomena of the three periods of time, from beginning to end, there is nothing that does not perish.”
Those who have attained penetration into the ultimate truth, the peerless beings of the world,
the wise ones possessed of insight and vision, and those who rescue and protect the world—
all are destroyed by impermanence; what person can endure forever?
Alas! Throughout the entire world, all living beings have fallen onto wrong paths.
At that time, Anuruddha was *aluludha* (unconfused) regarding the world;
having extinguished *aluludha*, he attained *niluludha* (tranquility) regarding birth and death.
I lament that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, and all living beings are left in total blindness and darkness.
This aggregate of conditioned formations is impermanent, like a light cloud drifting by;
arising swiftly and ceasing swiftly, the wise do not cling to it.
The adamantine thunderbolt of impermanence destroys the mountain-king of the Muni.
How base is the world’s frivolity, which shatters what is not firm!
The violent lion of impermanence harms the great seer, the dragon-elephant.
Even the Tathāgata’s Vajradhvaja is subject to impermanence and destruction;
how much more so for those who have not yet abandoned desire—how could they not feel dread?
Six seeds and a single sprout are all moistened by the same rain of water.
The four nutriments are its deep roots; the two edges and five kinds of fruits,
with the three periods of time as one single essence— this great tree of afflictions the Great Sage,
like an elephant, has uprooted, yet he could not escape impermanence.
Like an adorned pheasant that delights in water yet swallows a venomous snake,
suddenly encountering a great celestial drought, it loses its water and perishes.
Like a swift horse brave in battle, having completed the fight, it returns with mastery.
Just as fire blazes when fueled by wood, yet extinguishes of its own accord when the wood is exhausted, so too is the Tathāgata:
having completed his work, he returns to nirvāṇa.
Like the light of the bright moon, he universally dispels the darkness of the world.
Sentient beings are all illuminated by it, yet it then hides behind Mount Sumeru;
the Tathāgata is likewise, for the light of his wisdom illuminates the dark realms.
Having dispelled the darkness for sentient beings, he then conceals himself on the mountain of Nirvāṇa.
His fame is a supreme radiance, universally illuminating the world;
he extinguishes all darkness, moving without pause like a swift current.
He skillfully guides his seven noble steeds as his host and retinue follow him on his journey.
The radiant Sun Deity enters the Yamaka mountains;
When the sun and moon are obscured by the five veils, Sentient beings lose their light.
Having finished the fire-worship of the heavens, There remains only blackened, withered smoke.
The Tathāgata has already withdrawn his radiance, and the world likewise loses its glory.
Having severed the hope for affection and craving, he universally accords with the aspirations of sentient beings;
once the aspirations of sentient beings are fulfilled, his task is complete and all hope ceases.
Freed from the bodily bonds of affliction, one attains the true path;
leaving behind the clamor of crowds, one enters a place of tranquility.
By means of supernormal powers, one travels soaring through the void, having forever cast aside the instruments of suffering.
The heavy darkness of delusion is dispelled by the light of wisdom;
the dust of afflictions is washed clean by the water of knowledge.
No longer returning again and again, one dwells forever in the state of eternal tranquility.
Extinguishing all birth and death, All revere and honor him;
Causing all to delight in the Dharma, He fills all with wisdom.
Completely consoling all, The virtues of all flow forth everywhere.
His fame pervades all things, and his profound illumination continues unto this day.
Among those who vie for virtue, he maintains a heart of compassion toward them;
he does not rejoice in the four gains, nor does he grieve over the four losses.
Skillfully restraining all sensory faculties, with all the sense organs fully clear and penetrating,
one purifies the mind to contemplate with equanimity, remaining unstained by the six objects of perception.
One attains what has never been attained before, achieving that which others cannot achieve.
With the waters of the various paths to liberation, you satisfy the empty thirst of beings.
Bestowing what others do not give, you likewise expect no reward;
with a body of tranquil and wondrous marks, you fully know all thoughts.
Unshaken by likes or dislikes, Its power overcomes all enmity;
The excellent medicine for all diseases, Yet it is destroyed by impermanence.
Among all classes of sentient beings, Their joys in the Dharma differ in their various ways.
Universally responding to all that is sought, he completely fulfills every aspiration.
